speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the government does not intend to ask parliament for authority to retain rental and eviction control on commercial accommodation after the expiration of the Continuation of the Transitional Measures Act, March 31, 1948.
The house will recall that on March 1 last, as part of the programme of orderly decontrol, certain items of commercial space, chiefly new commercial buildings, commercial buildings rented for the first time or for a term of three or more years, as well as commercial space which had been sublet, were removed from control.
At the same time a provision was made which would enable the landlord of any com-

Questions
mercial space to obtain a 25 per cent increase of the maximum rental by offering to his tenant a two-year renewal lease on certain terms and conditions. These measures provided a free bargaining opportunity with respect to a substantial proportion of commercial space, and experience has indicated that many landlords and tenants have taken advantage of it. It is now felt that it will be possible to effect complete decontrol of commercial accommodation next spring.
Amendments being made to wartime prices and trade board rental regulations to take effect immediately will remove from control vacant lots used for motor car parking or sales, as well as gas stations owned by oil companies.
In the field of housing accommodation the only change made provides for the removal of rental and eviction control from all new houses, apartments, duplexes and other self-contained buildings completed after January 1, 1947. This is felt to be desirable as an encouragement for the construction of housing accommodation for rent at a time when it is so urgently needed.
Mr. TUST'IN: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister a question on the statement he ha^ just made? Is there to be no relief until next-spring for returned veterans to secure their own properties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: RENT CONTROL
speechtext: As I said a little while ago, the whole question of any possible relaxation of rental control with respect to necessitous cases has been under consideration for some time and is still under consideration. I am not yet in a position to make any statement as to what the result may be.

It was with a dull thud, Mr. Speaker, that we turned back to the bill itself to see how far this puny measure fell short of the glowing description of it given by the minister. Again we are driven back to meditate upon the contrast between the fine words used by government ministers and the sorry performance that we see in actual fact, the usual contrast between the glowing praise they heap upon their measures and the disappointing reality of those measures themselves.
In the present measure, Mr. Speaker, we have a bill which will not only disappoint this house, if the house is free in all quarters to express its true opinion, but will bring profound disillusionment to many people in this country who had been ted to expect some-

Old Age Pensions
thing really substantial in the way of justice for our aged pensioners. They had been led to expect great things by the government's own propaganda.
There has been a great build-up for this measure. It has been going on for a long time, but it has been proceeding at an accelerated pace since the speech from the throne. Nearly five months have passed since we listened to that speech on January 30 of this year, when the government first announced this measure to bring relief in the form of increases to old age pensioners, and here, after waiting for five months, we are offered this puny bill, a meagre installment on account of the lavish promises of the government.
What has been done in the light of this bill is to perpetrate a cruelty upon old age pensioners in this country who were led to expect from it a reasonable measure of help. I wish to return to a theme I touched upon briefly yesterday, because in this bill, and in the reasons given by the minister in his speech yesterday for seeking the support of the house for the measure, we see the government turning its back upon a position which has been recognized by parliament and by succeeding governments since 1931, namely, that the primary responsibility with respect to old age pensions and the provision of those pensions rests upon the federal authority and not on the provinces.
I refer to the fact that that principle has been embodied in our statute law since Mr. Bennett put it there in 1931; seventy-five per cent of the pension has been paid at the expense of the federal treasury. But in what the minister had to say yesterdajq a clear attempt was betrayed^-

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that the speech of the minister revealed an apparent determination on the part of the government to cast responsibility on the provinces with respect to meeting the needs of our aged people. What is the situation under this bill? Yesterday wre heard, from both the minister and the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), words of praise heaped upon the provinces which have been going farther than others in supplementing the inadequate old age pension to which the dominion has been
contributing. Why? These are the provinces which were pictured by the minister and the hon. member for Spadina as setting an example which ought to be followed by the other provinces. In other words, the provinces are now to be asked to assume the ultimate responsibility with respect to old age pensioners. It is implicit in what was said yesterday in this house by the minister and the hon. member for Spadina, that the pension-even with the slight increase offered in this bill to the pension to which the dominion will contribute seventy-five per cent-is inadequate and therefore the provinces must make good any inadequacy. In holding forth that contention I say that this government is turning its back upon a principle which succeeding governments have acknowledged and which parliament has recognized ever since 1931.
Not only that, but this government is turning its back on and making a complete retreat from the proposals which it made to the dominion-provincial conference in 1945. The leading feature of those proposals with reference to the provision for the needs of the aged that the dominion should assume full responsibility for providing a pension of $30 a month without a means test to every person seventy years of age and over in Canada. Where is that principle today? This government has turned tail, has cast aside that principle and has made a complete retreat from it. It is absolutely idle for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to stand in his place, as he did yesterday, and have the temerity to say to this house that the government is keeping within the framework of its proposals of 1945. The fact is that this government has cast that principle and these proposals overboard and has beat a retreat from them.

There is in the bill before us another illustration of this retreat. Is it realized by the house that by inviting the provinces, as the dominion still does in this bill, to supplement an inadequate old age pension contributed to in part by the dominion, the dominion is saying in effect that if the result of the old age pension with the provincial supplement and earnings is to bring the pensioner's income to over $600 a year, the reduction which will be made does not fall on the provincial supple-
Old Age Pensions

ment, does not fall on the earned income, but comes off the dominion pension? Let us take an example of that. Suppose an old age pensioner earns $250 a year at odd jobs. The maximum pension is $360. Let us say the province in which he lives contributes a supplement of $5 a month, or a total of $60 a year. The total income of that pensioner would be $670 over the year. What becomes of the $70? That is taken from him. Is it taken off the provincial supplement? No; it is taken off the pension to which the dominion is contributing; and the more . the provinces contribute by way of supplement in a case such as this where a pensioner earns some additional income, the more they are contributing to a reduction of the dominion pension. That is a fine state of affairs.

We shall not soon forget, Mr. Speaker, that the dominion government increased by $5 a month, by order in council in 1943, the old age pension which then was only $20 a month, only after they had been driven to it by demands from all parts of the country. The same situation exists today. This meagre advance which they have proposed in the pension has been brought about only as a result of widespread demands throughout the whole country. Apparently it must remain for those who sit on this side of the house, as well as for informed opinion throughout the country, to drive this government as long as it is in office and then

As I sat here yesterday afternoon listening to the discussion I wondered if once again the old people of this country were going to be deluded bj' some of the speeches delivered by the opposition the other day; if once again this important subject was going to be made a football by the opposition, in an attempt to ride into office on the backs of our senior citizens. moment, because I have something to say about their speeches. They may say it has not been expediency, that it has not been pressure, that it has not been because of this bill. Mr.-REID:	To continue with what the
leader of the official opposition stated yesterday, in my opinion the half truths that were stated by him and by the speaker who followed today are more dangerous than whole truths. They may be termed by them political truths, but in truths' name it is not true, because here is the statement made by the minister on behalf of the government, at page 4283 of Hansard for yesterday:	.
It is important at this stage to recall the proposals the federal government made in August, 1945, to the provinces with respect to a programme covering national health, public investment and social security. These proposals include a suggested scheme for a national old age pensions and old age assistance programme of a fundamental character.
Then on another occasion he said:
Pending final consideration of these proposals at_ the appropriate time, when it is possible to join with the provinces in consideration of our joint social security responsibilities, it is not the desire of this government to embark upon any programme which would jeopardize in any way the eventual implementation of these objectives.
In the face of those words how can any man honestly say there is now any reversal of government policy in this bill? It simply is not true; it is not according to the facts. I well remember listening to the great debate from across the other side of the house regarding what we were doing to the provinces when we suggested we should go to London and ask for a change in the British North America Act. Each and every member of this house knows that under the British North America Act the provinces have certain rights and jurisdiction, and, as the minister rightly says, they are extremely jealous of them. Would the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, if he were sitting on this side of the house, deliberately do other than this government has done? Oh, no; the speeches that he would make if he were in office would be far different indeed. So I say to hon. members that they should not be carried away too much by some of the utterances which have come from the opposition so far.
Now I want to say a word or two with regard to the leader of the C.C.F. party. An hon. member reminds me about the promises that were made by Mr. Bennett. I am not going to talk about those promises; I am not going to hold the leader of the Progressive Conservative party to promises made by others years ago. Those promises could be quoted, but I am not going to waste time doing so, because that is all water under the bridge, and I believe there are more important things to speak about. To come to the statements made by the leader of the C.C.F.

party, I agree with some of the things he said. In his opinion the pension should be the same in every province, and I entirely agree. Personally I think it should be national in scope. But the hon. member did introduce a remark about New Zealand, about the low cost of houses to rent in that country, and so on. Conditions in New Zealand is one subject to which I have given a little study. The other day I made a suggestion which I thought perhaps the hon. member had taken to heart, but evidently he did not. I suggested that the true guide in relation to actual costs in a country is how much labour a man has to expend for a suit of clothes, for his food, and so on. Yesterday something was said about the low rentals being charged in New Zealand. Well, one has only to remind hon. members that New Zealand farmers are getting far lower prices for their butter fat than are the farmers in this country, and have to pay two or three times as much for their machinery as our farmers pay. I have before me the official records, in case anyone doubts my statement. The price of butter in Canada at the present time averages 40 cents per pound. I have in my hand the latest dairy records of the dairy association of New Zealand, which is an official publication, and there the average price is around 31-48 cents per pound.

speechtext:
Well don't interrupt so much. I will take you on with respect to New Zealand and a comparison with the country any time. I am proud of Canada and conditions generally here.
Then mention of Great Britain was made by the leader of the C.C.F. There again the same thing enters into the picture. I have before me the last statement of wages paid to the people in London. This is an official record right from Britain. I shall not take up a great deal of time to deal with it, other than to say that the highest wages paid to metal engineers in the shipbuilding trade works out at around S100 to $110 per month. Compare that with the wages paid in this country to our mechanics-and when doing so let us not overlook the fact that in England they work 47-4 hours a week compared to an average of only 44 hours.
I now pass on to something else. We are all I trust in favour of lowering the age limit somewhat, and increasing the pension further. But certain facts must be faced. None of us is entirely content with what the government has brought down, but we realize nevertheless that it will be of great assistance to our aged people. At this point I am going to urge upon
the minister something which I am surprised to say has not thus far been mentioned in the debate. I suggest that when seven provinces of the dominion have come to a financial agreement with the federal government, steps should be taken then by the government to implement complete social security. I ask that, and I feel sure that if that step were taken the other two provinces would not be long before they joined.
Something should be said about the means test. Anyone who has spoken to our senior citizens realizes that the means test is one of the things which should be certainly done away with. I realize it is of no use to tell our aged citizens that in all countries in which we find a system such as we have in Canada, the means test prevails. There is no country-and this includes Great Britain, Australia and 'New Zealand, and all other countries which have social security measures-which does not have the means test. Personally I am in favour of doing away with it, because I believe that the sooner we get to complete social security for all our people, the better it will be for all.
I believe the heaviest burden falls on the women of this land. I am sure every hon. member has met women of fifty, sixty or sixty-five years who are ill or whose husbands have passed on and left them in straitened circumstances. There is no hon. member here who has not met persons who have not dissipated their earnings, or what little means they had, but who in after years have found themselves dependent upon their families or on charity. In many instances there are no families upon whom they can depend, and so must depend upon some organization to help or tide them over to the end. I am sure every hon. member could say he has met with many cases such as I have described. Therefore I say no one person, or no one member of any party, should claim that his party is the sole champion of the unfortunate and the aged.
I look forward in the near future to a far better deal for our aged citizens. For a moment of two I shall place before hon. members a few important figures. According to the latest figures given by the income tax branch, out of a total of 4,101,980 workers receiving incomes, 3,449,990 earn $2,000 or less per year. In other words, if one goes further into these figures he finds that only fourteen per cent of the people are earning between $2,000 and $5,000. Then, those who talk about soaking the rich must bear in mind that while perhaps there are a few well-off people in this country, the number is not as great as some would have us believe. There
Old Age Pensions

are about 47,000 with salaries ranging between S5.000 and $10,000 a year; and 14.307 with salaries between $10,000 and $25,000. Those with more than $25,000 number only 2,750.
I am not particularly interested however at this time in the higher income brackets, because the income tax branch takes care of them-it takes care of them fairly well indeed. However I am more interested in those in the low income groups. We find that in 1943 there were 524,696 earning less than $1,000. To me those are startling figures. I cannot visualize a young man marrying and raising a family under those circumstances, who could find himself with anything at all left to take care of his old age.
I say that when one realizes these facts he cannot help rising in his place in the house to champion the cause of the less fortunate who have never had enough in this life to save for their later years. I should like at this point to read one paragraph from a letter-and I believe it should be read, because to my mind it is important. First of all may I say the giving of pensions as a means of social security is a good thing particularly because it lengthens the lives of those who are up in years. The letter I have before me is from Mr. Creighton, who is in charge of the administration of old age pensions in British Columbia. He says:
On more than one occasion observant officials of old age pensioners' organizations have remarked that the lives of many of their members have definitely been lengthened by the receipt of the pension. They assert with evident conviction that this is due to the added sense of security which even this modest income gives them. These expressions of opinion, and the awareness of the rapid lengthening of the lifespan of people generally, interested us in doing some research work to find out how well British Columbia pensioners really are doing relatively in the race for longevity.
He proceeds to point out that a survey was made, and it was found that in 1928, the year the pension was first paid in British Columbia, there were 210 male pensioners who died at an age of about seventy-seven years. In 1944 the figures show that of 810 male pensioners who died, the average age was something more than seventy-nine years. They come to the conclusion from these figures that the pension has had the effect of adding about two years to the lifespan of these aged citizens.
One could go on setting out the benefits of social security measures, and especially old age pensions to our senior citizens. Another striking example of what social security can do is found when one looks at the life span
[Mr. Reid.)
of members in the other place. I have seen them go in there sick and half bent over, so much so that you would think they would not last long, and the week after theil appointment you would hardly recognize them; the way they would revive was just wonderful. It seems to lengthen their span of life. If that can be done for those who in most instances are fairly well off, just what will it do for the under-privileged1?
I am sorry in a way that the leader of the Progressive Conservative party made a comparison between raising the members' indemnity and old age pensions. However, I noticed that he did not get up and denounce the increase when it was brought in, nor did he say that he would not take it. Nor did I hear him say one word about the $2,000 being tax exempt. I am willing to go just as far as he, and if he w'ants to have it taxed I will support him. I believe it should be taxed. But he never said a word. Now he gets up and makes a comparison which I think is not exactly fair.
As to increasing pensions the question may be asked: Can we afford it? Of course we can afford it. In Switzerland they have a wonderful philosophy. In that country they sacrifice something in peace time rather than wait until a war comes. This country of ours made great sacrifices during the war and did its full share. Perhaps it did not do as much as Great Britain and other countries, nevertheless our people rose to the occasion during the war. If we had the philosophy of Switzerland and were willing to do a little more in peace time, I believe our nation would be the better for it.
Let us look also at our bank balances. I am not saying that bank balances represent our true wealth, because after all, real wealth consists of labour and material things. In 1939 there were 4,846,000 depositors with $2,530,200,000 standing to their credit. In 1947, in spite of all the cry against this government that we had gone to the demnition bow-wows, some 6,902,000 depositors had to their credit $5,803,445,396, more than double the amount of 1939. When one considers those figures one cannot but come to the conclusion that this country can afford more for our aged. We have afforded it for our children; why not afford it for our aged people?
In British Columbia the unemployment insurance people made a survey of those seeking employment, and they found that life is getting more difficult for people in the forty-five years and over age group; it is harder for them to get employment. Perhaps we are losing sight of the principle that the life of every individual who reaches a certain age

Old Age Pensions
should be used, not just spent. We are not doing our duty fully by providing old age pensions alone. I believe we are drifting to the time where the aged people may become the forgotten men and women. We will have to take note of the conditions under which they live, and of course provide an adequate amount upon which they can live.
Because of superannuation and annuity schemes many business concerns today are reluctant to engage people who are forty-five years of age or over. In the government service, where superannuation applies to all permanent employees, age may be a determining factor in employment. There is a place in life for people of all ages, provided they are competent. I have just been reading a booklet put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare which is under the jurisdiction of the minister in charge of this bill, from which I should like to quote as follows:
Fitting the older worker into gainful employment is becoming more urgent every year as the age composition of our population changes. In .1971, it is estimated that more than five million Canadians will be over 45 years of age. At that time, 36 per cent of the population will be in this age group as compared to 26 per cent today.
I think we could very well take stock of what has happened in Great Britain. In that country it has been estimated that only some eighteen per cent of the workers are carrying the entire nation-a staggering figure. I am warning the people of this country not to let us go so far in that direction that our younger people will be carrying the entire nation. We must take steps to see that useful employment is provided for all who are able to work. The very fact that superannuation and annuity schemes are becoming so popular is evidence that the people of this country are social security minded. I am just afraid that we may be drifting in the same way as Great Britain has drifted. Some evidence was given before the immigration committee, and if hon. members wish to look this up they will find it on page 207 of the proceedings of that committee of Wednesday, May 14. A most interesting table was given by Mr. Forsey of the Canadian Congress of Labour, I believe, which shows that in 1921, 2-8 per cent of our population were seventy years of age and over and that by 1941 this percentage had increased to four per cent. I merely mention these things to bring home to our people that something more than merely providing pensions will have to be done. We shall have to take stock also of a class of our citizens who are below sixty or sixty-five years of age and who are unable to find employment
because of the age limit restrictions of superannuation schemes which have been put into effect by dominion and provincial governments and many industrial employers.
I see my time is going on, but before resuming my seat I want to say that in my opinion we should have or aim at an old age pension of not less than S50 per month and $75 per month retirement allowance under a social security scheme. No one in the house has ever quoted figures to show whether $40, $50 or $60 is enough. There are some in receipt of pensions who may be able to get by nicely, but there are many of our citizens who have rent to pay, who have food and clothing to buy who certainly cannot get by in our towns and cities on less than $50 a month or more.
I have no apologies to make for getting up in my place and advocating increased pensions for senior citizens, which should be the same in every province. The rate of $50 a month is not too much and that should be our aim, with at least $75 a month under a social security scheme for those who are deprived of employment, with the means test removed and with a lowering of the present age limit.

I am glad to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare make that interjection. In other words he knows himself that it cannot be done, as does every hon. member. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that after you have used such words as the minister used yesterday, when in one place he said "ultimately" and in another place he talked about long range plans, about moving stage by stage and not upsetting the balance of the social security plans, about doing things within an over-all framework, and so on-after you have heard all these words, after you have listened to the pounding of desks, such as we heard during the remarks of the last speaker,
Old Age Pensions

the plain fact still is that we have before ns a proposal for an old age pension which is disappointing and utterly inadequate to enable our elder citizens to live in comfort, indeed to live at all.
Last year the present minister of national health and welfare was Secretary of State. In that capacity he had the honour and the privilege of piloting through this house an historic piece of legislation which makes it possible for us to be known as Canadian citizens. It seems to me that he should be hanging his head in shame to have to bring into the house this 3'ear a proposal that Canadian citizens, when they reach the age of seventy, be asked to live on $30 a month. It is an insult to citizenship; it is an insult and an affront to the members of parliament to bring such an inadequate measure before us. The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows, as well as all the rest of us in the house do, that this amount is inadequate^ and I am sure that he knows from experiences of his own how distressing poverty is in the lives of old people. I am certain that in the cabinet he must have fought for something better than this. It seems to me that he should not be willing to continue in a government which asks him to stand by a measure so inadequate.
During the past number of months we have had a great deal of publicity leading up to this measure. We had the promise in the speech from the throne on January 30 that the Old Age Pensions Act was to be amended, and then we had a definite promise from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on February 4. On that occasion he was not able to tell us just when this measure would be before us, but he did say that when it came down it would include all that we had then, on February 4, and something more. Well, I suppose there are those who will argue that S30 is more than $25; but as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, in terms of the cost of living today as compared with what it was a few months ago, $30 today is not worth as much to old people as $25 was on February 4. I submit that in practice that promise has been broken. Our old people are not to get more than they had on February 4. In terms of food, clothing and shelter, they are to get less than they had then. It seems to me, therefore, that this was no occasion for the boastful kind of speech we had from the Minister of National Health and Welfare yesterday; it was an occasion on which he should have come into this house in sackcloth and ashes.
The bill which is before us and the speech which was made yesterday by the minister

make two obvious admissions. Those two admissions are made in two ways. First of all there is the admission that $30 a month is not enough. That admission is made by the fact that the ceiling on the total income of old age pensioners is raised by this bill to $50 for a pensioner living by himself and to $90 for a married couple. I submit that these figures, $50 for a single pensioner and $90 for a couple, should be made by this government not a ceiling but a floor. The government should be coming before this house with a proposal to guarantee that our Canadian citizens, given the right last year to call themselves such, when they reach the age of not seventy but at least sixty-five should be guaranteed that for the rest of their days they will not fall below the standard of living which could be obtained at these figures.
The admission that $30 a month is not enough is also made in the appeal that the Minister of National Health and Welfare made yesterday to the various provinces. He appealed to the provinces that already have certain supplements in effect to continue these supplements; he appealed to other provinces to add to the $30, a frank admission that this government is not discharging its responsibility to our elder citizens, because he asked that the provincial governments take on part of that responsibility.

In connection with the relations that the bill proposes to be made with the provinces, I may say that this strikes me as one of the worst features of the legislation that is now before us. I find it difficult to reconcile this feature of the legislation with the loud preaching about Canadian unity that we get from the benches opposite. For several years now the provinces have been telling their old people who have appealed to them for higher pensions that the responsibility rested with the federal government, and in that contention I say the provinces are right. But because the federal government has been so slow in coming through with any kind of increase, provincial governments of all political stripes have had sufficient moral responsibility to their people to realize that they had to do something for them pending action by this government. And so in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia- Conservative, Liberal, C.C.F., Social Credit, and coalition-we have had an attempt by provincial governments to fill in the gap and give their people something pending the time when this government may act. Each time these governments have made it clear to their people that these were temporary grants that they were making until such time as responsibility was really recognized by the federal government.
At long last we got this year, in the speech from the throne, the promise that the Old Age Pensions Act would be amended, and our elder citizens across the country, particularly in the western part of Canada, which I know best, took heart. They felt that at last the responsibility for them, which rightly belongs here at Ottawa, was being recognized.
Now what happens? The government comes down with a proposal for a basic pension of $30 a month, and the minister stands in the house and admits that $30 is not enough to live on-he admitted it today again by an interjection in the course of my speech a few moments ago-but appeals to the provinces to make additions to the pension to bring it to $31.75 or $33.75, or $40 or $50 or whatever it really ought to be. This is not only an admission that $30 is hopelessly inadequate. It is a course that helps to bring about disunity in the country. The only fair and sensible basis for dealing with this matter in a country like Canada is to recognize the complete federal responsibility for old age pensions. I shall have a little more to say about that in a moment, but before I do I
Old Age Pensions

want to express my deep regret and bitter disappointment that the government not only failed to raise the amount to something adequate, but failed to meet some of the other pressing demands in connection with our elder citizens.
The failure to abolish the means test is utterly reprehensible on the part of this government. The failure to bring down the age has no logical justification at all; and, as other members have been rightly pointing out during the course of the debate, the failure to recognize the need for other services simply throws out of court completely all claims which the minister and all his colleagues make to any interest in social security and human welfare. It is just so much talk. The least they could have done would have been to bring in some sort of plan for medical services for our old people. As a matter of fact, that is one of the main features that were included in the petition which the leader of this group laid on the table of the house some weeks ago, signed by over a quarter of a million citizens, for it included a request for free medical, hospital and dental care.
I have done a little figuring in connection with this matter on the basis of what the experience of the Saskatchewan government has been in providing these services to the old age pensioners in that province. My reason for mentioning this is not to get into a political debate but to show what it would cost to meet this request, and how niggardly the government is in failing to come through with it.
Since the government of Saskatchewan instituted free medical, dental, optical and hospital care for all old age pensioners in that province, they have found that it costs an average per pensioner of $33.70 a year. I would like to break that figure down.

What we have before us is a bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act, which is supposed to concern itself with the welfare of Canada's old people. I find, according to the census of 1941, that in that year the total number of Canadians sixty-five years of age and over was 767,815 and the total number of Canadians in 1941, seventy years of age and over, was 450,091. I am taking this figure of seventy years and over, rather than sixty-five, because it is the figure that the government still has in the bill. I am suggesting that this bill should have included provision for completely free medical care at least for the 450,091 Canadians who are seventy years and over. I know, although I have not the exact figures before me, that the number in that bracket has increased since 1941. I would suggest a round figure of 500,000, which I am sure is liberal. On the basis of the experience in Saskatchewan, where completely free medical services have been provided at a cost of $33.70 per old age pensioner, this means that it would cost only $16,850,000 to provide completely free medical, hospital, optical and dental care for all Canadians seventy years and over.
What the hon. member who preceded me has said about t'he longevity that comes from security applies particularly to the value of having medical care. I suggest that what it would mean to all our Canadians who are seventy years of age and over to have the guarantee of all the medical and hospital care they need simply cannot be measured by such a small sum as $16,850,000. Even if the government sticks by the bill the way it is and refuses to accept some of the amendments we should like to see made to it, I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in his capacity as head of the department, will give consideration, even after this bill is passed, to implementing such a programme of free medical services for our elder Canadian citizens. Even if that benefit were given to all those sixty-five years of age and over, on the basis of the figure of 767,815 which I have given, it would still cost only $25,000,000 a year.
I now come back to the question of federal responsibility for old age pensions. I look upon old age pensions not as a form of charity and not as a social service. It is largely because it has been viewed in that light that

Old Age Pensions
people have argued about provincial responsibility. It is rather a matter of security; it is a matter of the rights of citizenship in a country the economic forces of which are controlled largely by the federal government. This has been coming into the thinking of our Canadian people and our leaders across the years. In the election of 1930, Mr. Bennett, then leader of the Conservative party, promised the electors that if he were returned to power he would raise the federal contribution to old age pensions from the fifty per cent, at which amount it was then, to one hundred per cent. In 1931 the government of the day brought before this house a measure to implement partly-and I suppose that is pretty good for an old party-the promise which had been made in the election of the year before. The amount was brought up to seventy-five per cent, but Mr. Bennett and his party are on record as believing that the federal government should pay one hundred per cent. In the course of that debate in 1931 the present Prime Minister called upon Mr. Bennett to implement his promise. I want to read one or two quotations from what the present Prime Minister said on July 27, 1931. First of all I quote from page 4197 of Hansard, and this is the present Prime Minister speaking:
So my right hon. friend need not regard any agreements existing at the present time as being either a bar to action or a cause for delay in implementing the pledge he made to the electorate that there would be a national old age pension system on a one hundred per cent basis.
He went on to quote from Hansard some remarks along the same lines made by Mr. Cahan, a former secretary of state, and then said this:
That, I think, is advice that might well be heeded at the moment.
A little later, at page 419S, the present Prime Minister, after proposing a dominion-provincial conference, said this:
Let the dominion, if so agreed, take over in its entirety the administration and control of old age pensions.
The present Prime Minister went on to say, in the second column on the same page:
I am just as strong an advocate of provincial rights as any person can be, but I do believe that the people of Canada sent us here not to represent the provinces but to represent the interests of the dominion.
In 1943 the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) who was then minister of finance and in charge of old age pensions, made a similar declaration in the course of a debate on that subject, as reported at page 5419 of Hansard 83166-279
lor July 24, 1943-this is the present Minister of Justice speaking:
I wish to say that I myself am in favour of old age pensions being within the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament.
Then we have had the Rowell-Sirois report, the whole point of which was that in view of Canada's economic structure, if we are to provide for Canadian, unity and minimum social standards, we must do some of these things on a national basis. That too was the meaning, as I take it, of the proposals made by the dominion government to the provinces in 1945. Yet now, after all this development of the realization that old age pensions, as a mark of the security that should go with citizenship, is a responsibility of the federal government, we have the minister coming in yesterday, on June 18, 1947, and proposing that this house approve an inadequate pension, and that, in turn, the provinces be asked to add to that in varying amounts. For example, he suggested that Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should pay a pension of $33.75. That would mean this government paying only 66 per cent of the total pension the pensioners would receive there, and the province paying 33 per cent. He also suggested that British Columbia might pay a pension of $38.75. There again, since this government's contribution would be only $22.50, that would be a split as between 58 per cent paid by the federal government and 42 per cent by the provincial government. Instead of moving on to 100 per cent the government is moving back toward the fifty-fifty basis, long since recognized as obsolete and unfair. Today the Minister of National Health and Welfare stood up and boasted of the fact that he has jockeyed the premier of Ontario into adding another $10 to the pension; in other words, that he has jockeyed Ontario into taking on part of this government's responsibility. I am glad that the people of Ontario are getting another $10. but I suggest it is a crime the way in which our old people are simply tossed back and forth from dominion to province and made the victims of a political football game, such as we have been having for months and years.

Yes; even in British
Columbia they might get better consideration than they have been shown thus far. But they are not going to get it by simply making our old people the victims of dominion-provincial or interprovincial warfare and competition. The responsibility rests here; and I am glad to see the minister wagging his head up and down, which means that he agrees with me.
When one talks about this question of federal responsibility the question also can be raised, what about the cost? I want to dip back into Hansard again. It is a very interesting institution, this business of Hansard recording in black and white the things hon. members have said. I find that back in 1943, at page 5420 of Hansard, the present Minister of Justice, then minister of finance, was replying to a request of the then hon. member for Burrard, now one of those fellows who have had their longevity stepped up by being put in the other place, and told him that in his view the provinces should take on this matter of increasing old age pensions because of the substantial surpluses they then had. Let me quote:
I do not think there is anything unreasonable or uneconomical or obsolete about the view that, when the provinces have changed their position from a combined deficit of perhaps $20,000,000 before the war to a combined surplus of from $60,000,000 to $70,000,000 today, while we have changed our position from a balance before the war to a deficit of over two billion dollars today, the people who have the primary responsibility should take the thing in hand.
That is the sort of remark the then minister of finance made a number of times during the war; I have the references here, but I will 83166-2791
not bother giving the rest of them at the moment. That was a position we all remember quite well; he kept telling us time and again, "Oh. the federal government has a deficit. The provincial governments have huge surpluses. They are the ones who should increase old age pensions." If that kind of argument was logical then, it is logical now. Remember, this year with great boastfulness the Minister of Finance told us this government was now reporting a surplus, not of sixty to seventy million dollars as all the provinces together had back in 1943, but a surplus of over $350,000,000. Well, if surpluses of those days in the provincial financial statements should have been turned into improved old age pensions, I suggest that a surplus of S350,000,000 in this government's financial statement should be turned into a much better deal for old age pensioners than they are getting under the bill now before us.
I see my time is nearly up, and I want to put in just a word in reference to the blind, about whom I shall have something more to say when we get into committee. It has been pointed out already by the leader of this group that the provisions for this particular class of Canadian citizens are hopelessly inadequate in this measure. As a matter of fact they should be covered by a separate measure entirely, and I hope that before long we will get to that stage in this country, for it is long overdue.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that this whole case which is being made in the course of this debate by members on all sides of the house should not be looked upon merely as. a matter of sympathy for old people. The statement has been made a number of times that no party has a mortgage on sympathy for our old people, and we all agree with that. The point I wish to make is that this matter of granting old age pensions should not be thought of as something that is done out of sympathy or out of pity for those sometimes referred to as "poor old folks." That is not the proper basis at all. Old age security is a matter of right, and what we should be building up here is a programme of security for all Canadian citizens; and our concern in this debate is not just for the so-called "aged poor"-I dislike that phrase immensely-who are now in their advanced years. We are also concerned about security as a symbol, as something that is achieved by Canadian citizens who live their lives here, who work and contribute to the wealth of Canada, and who have something to look forward to in their declining years. It is a
Old Age Pensions

symbol of something that can offset the fears, the insecurity, the feeling of frustration that comes over so many human beings when they realize that life consists of working from one depression to another and never having anything very sure to look forward to. The importance of this debate, the importance of old age pensions, as I have already stated, involves sympathy for our old people but it goes far beyond that. What we should be doing is building security. I contend that either we build security in this country or thousands of Canadians have died in vain. Either we build security or our way of life becomes too vulnerable to last in the kind of world w'e are in today. For the sake of democracy and freedom nothing is more important than that we establish security for Canadian citizens, for all our citizens. There is no better place to begin than with old age. The present government has failed to do that, but the fight for security goes on.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the introduction of bill No. 339, to amend the Old Age Pensions Act, it was my fervent hope that the bill would be of such a character as to render unnecessary a prolonged debate. Unfortunately my hopes have been shattered tragically. I was also hopeful that the changes proposed in the Old Age Pensions Act would render it unnecessary for us to engage in certain types of debates which from time to time have already cropped up.
I sincerely hope that throughout the remaining hours or days of the debate-whatever time may be registered-we can at least keep this matter wholly and completely above the realm of party politics. It has been said, and rightly so, that no party has a monopoly on the interests and welfare of our pioneer citizens. But we all have a responsibility, and I for one fervently hope that that responsibility will be recognized and carried out. Possibly I was too optimistic when I assumed that since this is the twentieth anniversary of the passage of the Old Age Pensions Act, and also the twentieth anniversaiy of the Prime Minister's acceptance of leadership of the government in Canada, some satisfactory legis-.ation would be placed before us. I thought hat in the light of these anniversaries, and }f the further fact that we have a new and young minister in charge of the bill, something would be brought forward which all of us could praise to the skies.
But I was altogether too optimistic. Only recently I decided to look back through history in an effort to determine whether or not we have made any reasonable progress in connection with the treatment of our pioneer

citizens. I found, sir, that we have made some progress because I learned that primitive peoples disposed of their aged in the simple and straightforward fashion of dashing out their brains with clubs. We have gone beyond that. I have learned further that among some primitive peoples it was the custom simply to abandon the old people and leave them to die. I was going to say we do not do that- and possibly I should not say that. We are modern, or at least pride ourselves upon our being modern. We pride ourselves, too, upon our civilization. We contend that we are progressive and that we are Christian. No, we could not tolerate such inhumane treatment as was accorded the old people of primitive time. Our developments render those means more or less impossible. It is essential that we apply methods which at least are less repulsive.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: But more barbarous.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Today, in effect, we say to our pioneers, "If you manage by hook or by crook to survive until you are seventy, you may become eligible for pension." I place emphasis upon the word "may"-all the emphasis at my command. Then there are provisos-and it is with respect to many of these provisos that I feel most bitter. And before proceeding further let me say that while I may not display a great deal of heat, it is not because I do not feel that way. By the utilization of a vast amount of control I manage to suppress some of the feelings I harbour.
I have said there were provisos of extreme importance, one of which is associted with the iniquitous means test. On previous occasions I have said that through the provisions of that test we pry into the most personal affairs in the lives of these people. It is a continuous process, too. Periodically we go back to pry-at least once a year, and in some instances more frequently.
The second proviso, associated with the first, is one which seems to indicate that if upon some previous occasion the individual did have a few hundreds or a few thousands of dollars, and neglected to invest the sum in an annuity, with the result that the money disappeared, that person is not eligible for pension. Recently no less than four cases in one community came to my attention. It so happened that some years ago these poor unfortunate people had some money

not a great deal, but some. They were asked why they did not keep it and why they did not invest it. Because the answers -were not satisfactory to the officials those people were completely deprived of pensions.

Old Age Pensions
Then there is another proviso which has to do with relatives of our older people. I know the act is not always administered in the way it could be, so far as the degree of viciousness is concerned; but when I learned that the department may go to the son-in-law of a prospective pensioner to ascertain whether he is in a position to support his father-in-law, it made me sick.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: And so it does everybody else.

speechtext:
I am sure it does. I recall not so long ago assisting an applicant in the preparation of his form. Perhaps I should not have done it, but after reading the form I became so much disturbed that I said, ''Write on it 'it's none of your damn business' ".
Then there is another proviso which is wrapped up with a multitude of baby provisos. This one refers to residential qualifications. I am not saying there should not be some residential requirements. But when I see some of the methods employed in a determined effort, so it seems, to deprive persons of their just dues on this ground, I am greatly exercised.
We come, of course, to the matter of establishing age. It does not matter whether a person is so old and decrepit he can barely move; it does not matter whether fifty persons looking at the individual would place his age at one hundred, he must still produce proof before the pension is paid. I remember an old lady of about seventy-five who for some reason or another could not procure a birth certificate. Evidently there was something lacking in the census record. Finally the officials said to her, "Well, there is still another door open to you. If you can find some one who was present at your birth and who can complete an affidavit to the effect that you were born on that occasion, then we will grant you a pension". Such a ridiculous thing! I suppose such an individual would have to be from ninety to a hundred years of age to be able to complete that affidavit. Just how many such persons were present at these births? They do not usually call in all the neighbourhood. How many can produce the evidence essential for the establishment of age?
I know that the pioneer citizen advances certain arguments in support of his right to pension. He points out that possibly for fifty years he has struggled in order to develop Canada. He may have gone into some undeveloped backwoods area and helped to bring that area into production to add substantially to the wealth of this great nation. He says, "I have played a most important part in putting Canada in a position where today her production is valued at SI0.000 million to SI 1.000 million." He also points out, as was indicated by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low') last night, that he has paid 820,000, $30,000 or $40,000 in taxes during the years he has been a resident of the country. He points out, and rightly so, that perhaps on one occasion he served in defence of this land, and he reminds us that in many cases his sons and his grandsons have also served in that capacity. It makes him bitter to realize that after all that, if he is still unable to provide for himself between the ages of sixty and seventy if he cannot meet all the conditions laid down and applied at the age of seventy, he is not receiving, from that land which he helped to build, justice in the smallest degree.
Many of these older persons point out that prior to the terrible depression they were in such a position that had things continued as they should have continued, they could have made adequate provision for their old age. Hundreds of them lost almost everything during those bitter years. They attained an age when they could not make recovery. Were it not for the fact that governments were responsible for the depression were it not for the fact that governments did not take the action they should have taken to alleviate the distress which prevailed at that time, his argument might not have been quite so good. He says, "I am willing to argue that I cannot be expected to secure and carry out my assignments in connection with employment." It is recognized by all reasonable persons, and it has been emphasized already in this debate, that competition in the labour market is becoming more intense all the time. Men over fifty years of age are finding it desperately hard to secure employment. Why should they, after all the working years they have put in, be expected upon attaining those ages to go out and seek work? I contend that their services are not required for the continued welfare of this country.
Then finally he says, "WTe found $20,000 million during the war for destructive purposes. We thought we were paying for it while it was being fought, but we find now that it has to be paid for completely." He says. "If that could be done, that which reflected the best productive capacity of this country, then surely Canada is in position out of the vast production of this day to make sufficient available to guarantee a standard of decency we deserve."
Old Age Pensions

Running parallel with those arguments are the observations of the officials to these persons and the rest of us. We are constantly advised of the great debt and the financial obligation of interest associated with it; we are told that Canada must honour these obligations, that we cannot add to this debt the amounts essential for the welfare of these people. That argument is advanced, and it is also pointed out that our present rates of taxation are tremendously high. They argue that we cannot possibly increase taxation if that is necessary-I say it is not-in order to make adequate provision for these persons. They endeavour to beat them down on that point.
They are told, "You cannot blame us for what you lost during the depression because that depression was an act of God." This man is told that his sons were adequately compensated, because they preserved their own freedom. He is told that he can find work if he 'wants it, I have heard that argument offered in connection with certain cases. He is told that the increasing proportion of older people in our population may later create an intolerable burden if we grant higher rates of pension to those who are now past sixty years of age. As a matter of fact, the same argument is used when we advocate increasing the pensions paid to those above seventy years.
Then we come to this extremely interesting argument that is advanced. It is said by government spokesmen, and the minister was as guilty as the others, that they expect that eventually their long-range programme will materialize and then these persons will be infinitely better off than they are today. That is small comfort for the individual who is in distress today. I am not one of those who contends that the government 'has abdicated the position which it formerly held in respect to this matter; I am not going to say that this bill is a reversal of government long-range policy. What I am saying is that it does not deal adequately with the problem which confronts us today.
The minister may talk all he likes about unemployment insurance, family allowances and veterans rehabilitation benefits, but he knows and I know that those things do not in any way alleviate the distress which is today facing so many of our older citizens. They may be part of an over-all long-range policy -they are commendable and I am not criticizing them-but for heaven's sake let us divorce them from the problem with which we are now confronted.
I have referred already to this question of proof of age. I sincerely hope the government will find it possible lo revise the regula-

Lions covering the establishment of age. When I look over the average payments by the provinces it fills me with horror. When you find these persons getting less than one dollar a day in actual cash it makes you wonder, especially when you realize that, all government statements to the contrary notwithstanding, the cost of living today as compared with pre-war years is completely staggering. Let us take food and clothing alone. I do not have to deal with these, but anyone should realize how hopelessly intolerable the situation is today, and goodness knows even during the pre-war years at the prevailing rates the situation was pretty hopeless too.
Those provincial governments which have extended medical, dental, optical, hospital and other services to their people are certainly to be commended, I do not care what the complexion may be. Possibly competition between provincial governments is a pretty fair thing. It seems to me that sometimes it is the only way that some persons do receive the justice which they deserve. But to those provinces which have not extended the services, I say, do it. If we are able to do it in the western provinces, the provincial governments elsewhere should be in a similar position, possibly not to extend the same degree of service, but certainly to extend some service in that respect to their people. I note too often when we talk about living costs-and I referred to it a moment ago-the old age pensioner has it indicated to him, directly or indirectly: Well, after all, the cost of living is pretty high and your pension is pretty low, but you should thank God you do not live in China. That is small comfort, but that, sir, is in effect one of the answers we constantly receive.
I do not like to hear hon. members continually going aboard to find that something there is better than or worse than something here. My philosophy is, let us make this country the very best. That is our concern. The thing that makes me feel very sad is the fact that these pensions are reduced in many cases on the slightest pretext. I cannot refrain from telling this story. In a community with which I am quite familiar we have an old gentleman of eighty-three years of age. He is a wonderful individual for that age. He is anxious to work; he does work; he has an old team of ponies; he has an aged cow. He has three or four chickens; possibly they have reached the maximum of production and just about laid the last egg. That old fellow goes out with the old team of horses. At Christmas time, for instance, when it was very cold, he peddled trees from door to door; he came to my house when the temperature was 40 degrees below zero. That man raised his own family and

Old Age Pensions
adopted two children. One of them is now around thirty years of age and served with distinction in the recent war. His little girl is eleven years of age. That poor old fellow's pension was cut down to $6.25 a month. After constant fighting we got it back. After quite a number of years I think it is now at the maximum. I know this is just one case, but I ask, is it isolated?.

On two or three previous occasions I brought up something in the house in connection with old age pensions, and I am still waiting for an answer. I trust that with a new minister the explanation will be forthcoming. I can at least expect an attempt to answer it. When a man becomes seventy years of age and qualifies for pension he will secure the maximum; let us say for illustrative purposes, that it is $30 a month, as it is in some places. If he has a wife who is under seventy, so far as the actual pension payment is concerned' she is completely ignored. In other words they as much as tell him he should not have been fool enough to get married. At least he should have married someone as old as he was-or she should. It works both ways. I wonder if, when they look upon a wife who happens to be sixty-five, they think that there might be still a couple of working years left in her. That is something I cannot understand. They completely ignore the presence of the wife ; because, if the man is a widower or bachelor he gets the same amount as though he were a married man. Of course, the old question of outside income might come in, but once again you can drown that as far as this bill is concerned.
I think I am safe in assuming that the citizenship qualification is to be eliminated, and that is a good thing. I understand there are to be modifications in the residential requirements, and I commend the government for that too. I understand also there will be a new arrangement for balancing off accounts as between the provinces, and that is proper. I commend the government for it. But that is about all that I can commend them for.
I regret that in this year 1947 we have not been able to offer our pioneer citizens something more than we are giving them. We have constantly boasted of what we are able to do in this country, and I may say to the government that they never hesitate when it comes to something that they consider it desirous of going ahead -with. Costs never seem to concern the government so far as some other things are concerned. They boast about the

great productive capacity of the country, and all that these people are asking for is an effective claim against enough of this production to enable them to live out their lives in decency.
I say that so long as this act remains on the statute book as it stands we had better keep our mouths shut. I have faith in the minister; I have not lost it all. I simply hope that he will within the cabinet shake things up as far as he can, even by using physical force, and I am sure the Minister of Labour will help him. I am not going to say more on this occasion. I am absolutely opposed to the present rate of pension. I expected the Minister of Labour to bite at that one. I thought he would say, "Well, are you going to vote against it?'' He realizes as well as I do that another $5 to the old age pensioner will mean something. I am not one to deprive the pensioner of another $5, although I feel mighty cheap in playing a part in offering him that paltry sum. I am unalterably opposed to the means test as one of the most vicious things. The Minister of Labour in 1933 dealt with that and said that the pension should be paid as a matter of right. In fact, he said, it is nobody's business what you earn. I commend the minister for that.

May I make one more observation before I conclude. If the minister reads my remarks with reference to the wife under seventy he will find that I did not change my position at all from the first statement I made. I said that from the standpoint of outside income the pensioner's position was improved. Even under the old bill, as far as outside income was concerned, his position was slightly better when he enjoyed the married status. But as far as the pension payment itself is concerned, the wife is ignored. I wonder how the women feel about a government which will simply write them off as it would a bad debt.

speechtext: I have had a great deal to do working -with the government of Alberta since I have been Minister of Labour and before that. speechtext:
I was thinking of Mr. X; let me put it that way. I have a vivid recollection of the agitation that took place right across the dominion in connection with the establishment of the principle of old age pensions. I am not going to go into the history of this matter. It was introduced by the Liberal government of that day. Other people can take all the credit they wish for the crystallization of public opinion in that regard. In my opinion, notwithstanding views to the contrary, the greatest contribution made to the establishment of old age pensions in this country, and in the education of the people which is necessary before any forwardlooking policy can be put into operation, came from the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and other labour organizations. I was closely associated with the trades and labour congress, and labour organizations can take an unpopular opinion and make it stick. May I say this with regard to political parties, and I do not exempt any political party in this House of Commons; as a rule, in a general way, they follow public opinion. But I remember the years of agitation until public opinion was crystallized and we established the principle of old age pensions in Canada.
This afternoon I mentioned, as I have mentioned before, that I was a witness to the agreement-signed by Hon. Howard Ferguson, a Conservative in the province of Ontario, and Hon. Peter Heenan, who was federal minister of labour-which established old age pensions in Ontario. Let us not wear our consciences on our coat sleeves. I think every self-respecting member of the House of Commons believes in the principle of old age pensions.

Old Age Pensions

But we went into the thing blindly, as one does in many things. I believe that any nation which over a long period of time gives away something for nothing is placing itself in jeopardy.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: You are not doing that in this country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Wait a minute. Do not forget that I supported the principle of a noncontributory old age pension plan at that time. I often talked the matter over with the late Tom Moore, with whom I was closely associated. I think one error in judgment which we made was that we did not adopt a contributory policy from the start, as a result of which the old age pensioner would get the pension by right and not on the basis of charity.

speechtext: I do not say this in a critical spirit, but I believe my Social Credit friends could render a service to the old people in Alberta if they would go back there and suggest to the government of Alberta that they follow the policy of the government of British Columbia, and, if I am given to understand it correctly, the policy of the government of Ontario, and raise the pension from $33.75, as I think it is there at the moment, to $40 a month, which it will be in those two provinces.

speechtext: And let the government here get out from under as regards responsibility.

My hon. friend talks about responsibility. That is an easy thing to say. He knows something about the constitution of this country, and you cannot laugh
it off. It is my frank and candid opinion that the fathers of confederation builded better than they knew. When one is in a corner and wants to get out from under, it is the easiest thing in the world to say that they did not. I am not offering this as a criticism, but I know of no provincial government which is more conscious of its constitutional prerogatives than the government of Alberta; and I agree with them. I do not believe that the Creator ever meant that we should all be cast in a common mould, in a nation as big as Canada.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Thank God for that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "Thank God for that", and I agree with him. I do not think we were ever intended to be cast in a common mould. I believe that there is strength in diversity and decentralization, which is, may I say-and I am not talking politically now-good sound Liberal policy and philosophy. There are those in this nation who would centralize everything. As I said before in this House of Commons, I was in Germany when Hitler put over his revolution. Any fool can govern a country with a bayonet in his fist as long as he does not stick it into himself. What happened there? Everything was centralized in Berlin. I point that out to t'he great centralizers who want to get out from under in this present argument, if they say that responsibility should be on a national basis rather than on a cooperative basis in connection with the matter now before the house.
I believe that in the light of experience it will be proven that the act passed in 1927 was a sound one. I do not think that any political party in this house has a first mortgage on ability or willingness to make provision for improved conditions for the people of this nation in the sunset of their lives. When the suggestions made to the dominion-provincial conference by this government are carried out -and we mean to carry them out-and when we move to a policy of old age pensions, with a reduction of age, based on the contributory principle, I believe it will be a tremendous step in the direction of a sane method of approaching this vital question in the life of this nation. We must remember this. With a contributory basis, there is the right to have some say in the administration of the money which has been contributed. We have heard a good deal about the means test, and I suppose we shall hear more about it. On a contributory basis, of course, the means test is not necessary because when a person contributes, he is justly entitled to the benefits of the plan. We have heard Great Britain
[Mr. Mitchell.1

Old Age Pensions
quoted in this debate. If newspaper reports are to be believed, only this week a member of the British cabinet-a former member of a labour government; a member of the government of Lloyd George in the first great war- is placed in the position of having to make a public issue of his own position because of the means test in Great Britain. They have the means test for non-contributory pensions at the moment. I am not talking about whether the principle is sound or otherwise. What is done in New Zealand and Australia has all been pointed out. But let me say this to my hon. friends. All these social matters -and I am all for them, and have been all my life-in effect mean the redistribution of the national income of a country. I do not believe that a nation can have a body of rich people-as we see in some countries of the world today-and a mass of poor people at the bottom, and maintain its equilibrium as a nation. That condition, by its very nature, spells revolution irrespective of the country in which it exists. As these great schemes of social advancement are placed in operation we must be prepared-and I myself am prepared; I speak personally now-to pay the bill through taxation, as is being done in Great Britain, as we are doing in the Dominion of Canada, and as is being done in New Zealand, Australia, or any other country where these reforms have been placed in operation in the last generation or so. We must be frank and honest with our people and tell them that these schemes mean the redistribution of the wealth of the nation and require willingness to bear taxation in order that they may be put into force. I know some people in this dominion think it can be done in some other way. I have no objection to listening to their theories, but of course I still believe two and two make four, though I left school at a very early age. In connection with any of these schemes; whether it be workmen's compensation, where there is an assessment on the employer on the basis of the risk in the particular industry, which, of course, in turn is paid by the public generally so that in effect it is a tax; whether it be children's allowances; whether it be old age pensions; whether it be unemployment insurance, of course in smaller measure because that is contributory; in the same breath that you speak, in my judgment-and I know this is not good politics-you must tell the people frankly that this redistribution of the wealth of a nation can be done only on the basis of taxation. Those members who say in this House of Commons that we should do this here and that there; who advocate increased old age pensions and increased unemployment insurance, as the hon. member 83166-280J
for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) did this afternoon, cannot in one breath demand a reduction in taxation and in the next breath increased expenditures by the government of this country, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has done.

The subject is too interesting; that is the trouble. And if I might say so, if my hon. friends would stop interrupting and just listen for a while, it would be better.
Primarily, the men who are responsible for the establishment of old age pensions in Canada were the trade unionists of this country. And when I say that I am taking no credit away from the late member for Winnipeg North Centre, or from any other member from Winnipeg or any other place, irrespective of party. Let us give credit where credit is due. Old age pensions in British Columbia were introduced by a Liberal government. In Ontario they were introduced by a Conservative government. In Quebec it was a Liberal government, again; and so on, across the dominion. Let us not play politics in this, but give credit where credit is due. I say to hon. members from every province in the dominion: Here is the contribution of this government. Let those hon. members go back to their own provinces and make to the provincial governments the same kind of speeches they have been making in the House of Commons in this debate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for a back-bencher to follow a minister, particularly after that minister has covered the field as widely as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has done.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
