speechtext:
It is also difficult for a back-bencher to rise in his place and be critical of his party. On most occasions, of course, it is the wise thing to keep silent, and do one's battling in caucus. However I should not like to remain silent on a matter which is of such great concern to the people of my province and of my constituency.
I can say to the minister who is piloting this bill through the house that the bill is a great disappointment to me, and it must be a very great disappointment to labour unions in my riding which have been such strong advocates of an improved scheme. And it must be a bitter, bitter disappointment to the old age pensioners of British Columbia.
Very high hopes were raised in that province and right across the dominion by the proposals in the green book of the dominion-provincial conference, which have already been referred to in this debate. I must admit that I stood on platforms and spoke with pride as to what the federal government would do in the way of better old age pensions, along the lines of what is contained in the green book. And so, when I find the present proposals so far from what was contained in the book I feel I must stand in my place, say my piece, and then, at the end, suggest what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) and I intend to do about the matter.
There are four major things wrong with the bill. They are the amount of the pension, the means test, the age limit and the failure now to begin to introduce a contributory pension scheme.
I need not go into these subjects,at length, because the basic principles have been repeated again and again for many years by all hon. members on all sides of the house. However adequate or inadequate the amount may have been before the war, I am sure no old age pensioner today could begin to provide for anything like an adequate standard of living on the pension proposed.
It is all very well to look back to 1926 when the government introduced old age pensions, and to say that it was never intended to be a living allowance, and that it was intended only to be as a supplement to the savings which an old person had managed to accumulate up to that time. But as the years passed, more and more attention has been paid to considering it as a total pension. The depression aided in this movement, be-
Old Age Pensions

cause few of our old people were able to save anything between 1930 and 1940, to provide for their old age.
So today at least in my province-and I am sure in many' other provinces-old age pensions are actually to the great majority of pensioners their total living allowance. The cost of living has greatly increased. We have seen the well organized trade unions fight for and receive substantial increases in their rates of pay, in an effort to compensate for the increase in the cost of living. And that cost of living affects the aged just as much as it does those who are today employed by industry or by the government.
More than that, as was pointed out recently by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) there has been a downward drop in interest rates on bonds and securities, a good thing for the country but which has affected those people who put their money into government and industrial bonds in the hope that the returns from them would be of assistance in their old age. Because of those two factors, I say the present proposal, so far as amount is concerned, is quite inadequate.
I need not say much about the means test. It has already been described as being offensive, not only because it carries the taint of charity, but because, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) there is a continual prying, again and again and again, into the personal affairs of these old people. Certainly it is a great discouragement to thrift, a point which was covered the other evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
There was brought to my attention a case which affected a postman in my constituency who had been retired on a pension of S52 a month. He was complaining bitterly that if he had not been so thrifty and had spent a little more on beer instead of contributing to the superannuation fund, upon his retirement he could have got what some of his fellow postmen were getting on retirement, a war veterans allowance of 860. He had applied and got the difference of SS. To him there had been absolutely no advantage to have, during the years in which he was working, tried on his own behalf to make some provision for old age, and not to rely upon charity.
I believe there is a growing tendency to rely too much on the state. Instead of encouraging this tendency with a means test, we should be going in the other direction and giving people encouragement to make their own plans for their old age. Certainly the

removal of the means test would be the first step to encourage people to make their own plans for their old age.
So far as the age level is concerned, the employment situation in Canada is not so good for people over the age of sixty-five, or even those over the age or sixty. We know that. The government itself, one of the greatest employers in the country, will not employ anyone anywhere near that age. Most industrial firms in Canada now recognize that at sixty-five years of age a. man's working days are practically over, and that the same applies to a woman at sixty. That is why industrial pension schemes set these age limits.
Then, there is one factor which makes the situation worse. There is the human factor that most men do marry girls a year or two, or perhaps more than that, younger. At the present time we have a situation whereby when the husband reaches the age of seventy he will draw a pension of S30, but his wife who is sixty-eight or sixty-seven years old will draw nothing. So that if they are destitute their total living allowance for the two of them is only S30 a month.
A few minutes ago the minister objected strongly to comparisons being made between this country and New Zealand, Great Britain and other countries. He said in that respect that by allowing the husband a little larger theoretical earnings we were compensating for it. I do not find it necessary to make that comparison. Let us look at our own legislation. We have another old age pension scheme in Canada which is known as the war veterans allowance, and referred to by the veterans as the burnt-out pension. The principle behind it is that service in combat prematurely ages a man. even though he suffered no wound in combat. As he becomes older, his nervous system shows the effects of shock and exposure to combat fighting. And so at the age of sixty we pay an old age pension to any man who has had combat service. When the man is sixty years old his wife collects too, and they receive the full burnt-out pension of 860, not 830. I suggest that it is not necessary to refer to New Zealand and Great Britain, but merely to look at the very good legislation passed by this government just last year in that respect, under the supervision of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), to get a precedent for paying double pensions to the husband, even if his wife is not yet sevent}'.
The point about which I feel most keenly in this whole statement is the failure to make any specific mention of the introduction

Old Age Pensions
of a contributory scheme. One of the excuses or defences against going ahead with a larger pension scheme is the enormous cost. We talk so easily in terms of millions and billions these days that at times we forget we are a comparatively small country in population and that our tax bill bears heavily upon those who pay income tax. The figures which were offered in this house for a $50 pension at sixty years of age were $800,000,000 a year. Last year there were about 2.000,000 taxpayers, so that would mean an additional $400 to be paid annually by every income taxpayer.
The figure mentioned yesterday by the leader of the opposition was $560,000,000 for a pension of $50 at sixty-five years. There again, with the reduced number of income taxpayers this year that would mean almost $300 extra for every income taxpayer in Canada. While that may be some defence it should not stop the consideration of an adequate old age pension, because the way it can be done is to inaugurate now a contributory scheme.
The excuse immediately offered is that it would take a constitutional amendment and that we made our promises to the provinces that in all these dominion-provincial agreements there would be no suggestion of an amendment to the British North America Act. I think we can carry that sort of thing too far. I see no reason why the people of western Canada and the maritimes should suffer because of the obstinacy of George Drew and Maurice Duplessis. The government is wearing these excuses a little thin. I am quite sure there would be a much better feeling throughout the country if the government in announcing this inadequate measure, had said, "It is just a stop-gap for we are now preparing legislation for a contributory scheme which the provinces can, if they choose, adopt, but which at least will be a start toward the payment of pensions on a decent basis." Most of the people in my riding that I know do not want charity from the government. The labour unions in my riding say that they are willing to pay for their pensions during the period of their working days. The sooner such a scheme is inaugurated, the sooner the large sums necessary will accumulate and a great part of the present load can be taken off the government exchequer.
I am speaking, of course, in a critical fashion on this bill, but I cannot join wholeheartedly with the remarks of some of the opposition members. I was not in the least impressed by the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). He ducked around, quite skilfully for him, what the Conservative
party would do. At the top of page 4294 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
. . . and it is further estimated that a plan covering people 65 years of age and over, at $50 a mouth with no means test, would cost this nation $560 million a year.
He gives no indication whether that is the committed policy of his party. More than that, he has a responsibility-after all, he is paid by the people of Canada to act as leader of the opposition-to suggest alternative programmes which are practical. He makes no mention of how that $560 million is to be raised each year, except by the old implication of the Tory party that it can be done by cutting out extravagance. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar rightly challenged him on that-his party has been challenged before -and on other occasions the only extravagance which the Tories suggested could be cut out was the travelling expenses of the national film board.

speechtext:
You can speak after I have finished. As the estimates come out, on every item I should like to ask the members of the Tory opposition and the members of the C.C.F., who have shown a little appreciation of the difficulties of raising money because they have authority in Saskatchewan; "How much of this $560 million are you going to save on this item;
Old Age Pensions

how much do you want to cut out?" Instead of talking loosely with a complete lack of responsibility, they should consider the matter in that way.
The attitude of the Tory party is best described by a phrase which I am quite sure the leader of the opposition thinks be used unfortunately. He accurately disclosed the Tory outlook toward our senior citizens when he called them the aged poor. That is certainly a return to the Tory policies of the middle eighteenth century with their poorhouse system.
More than that, there are two provincial governments in this country which are Tory run, one openly and one under another name. Let them begin to measure up to what the poorer western provinces are doing, and then there will be some justification for the many remarks they have been making. We will watch with great interest when the estimates come up for the great slashes which the Tories have promised so that they can find $560 million a year with which to pay $50 at sixty-five years, without any increase in taxation.
The C.C.F. were a little bit more guarded. The real leader of the opposition is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He has a little more expectation of being in this seat over here at some time in the very distant future. As I say, he was a little more guarded. He was not as explicit as the Minister of Labour, who got right down to the crux of the matter-taxes.
Out in British Columbia the C.C.F. are also quite guarded. Generally the C.C.F. in British Columbia are the revolutionaries of the party. That is the word they like to use. They are the great promisers. This spring they held a convention to which I have already referred. Colin Cameron, at one time member for Comox, was elected president. They discussed old age pensions at great length. Some of their delegates suggested, just like some C.C.F. members here have suggested, that we in the province should go ahead and give a $15 to $20 bonus. Mr. Winch, the British Columbia leader, answered, and I quote from the Comox District Free Press-this is interesting because this paper is published in the home town of the president of the C.C.F. in British Columbia-of Thursday, April 17, where he is replying to the suggestion that the C.C.F. as a provincial unit should pledge themselves to go on and increase the provincial old age pensions contribution. I quote:
At the convention, house leader Harold Winch, referring to old age pensions, cautioned against committing a future C.C.F. government to permanent bonuses for which finances would have to be found.

speechtext:
His friends at that convention did not think so. It was being urged that the provincial bonus should be supplemented. That is what they were wanting to do, but Mr. Winch seemed to think the mantle of leadership of the government was about to fall upon his shoulders and he was very guarded. That is the only reason I can think for the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar being a little more guarded than the hon. member for Neepawa, on where the money was to come from.
A great deal has been said about the generous pensions paid in New Zealand and Great Britain, the inference being that those socialist countries are the only ones which can provide a decent pension. I am amazed that no mention has been made of the pensions paid in the western states of the United States of America, which, after all, is the last great home of private enterprise, such as Washington, Oregon, California and, above all, Colorado. Colorado has a basic pension of $45 a month which is paid for by taxes on racing and liquor, two admirable sources from which to provide old age pensions. They have a most excellent system-my source of information is the Canadian Press account of last Christmas, which I do not doubt-under which they do not allow any funds to accumulate from year to year. At the end of each year they declare a bonus out of the accumulated surplus, and this year the bonus was $220 per old pensioner. The result was that the pension paid in Colorado amounted to S63.30 a month. Therefore I do not think a government has to be socialist in order to pay an adequate old age pension.
Having been a little critical of the government and the government's proposals, as well as of the remarks of the Conservative and C.C.F. parties, I think it is only fair that I should say at this time how I think the pension should be paid for. I believe it would have been a most excellent start to have brought in today the actual proposals which were made in the green book. The fact that Drew and Duplessis do not agree is neither here nor there. Seven provinces have agreed, and I am sure that if that offer had come forward the others would have agreed. The federal payment would be $30 as of right without any means test, at seventy, and I am quite sure that my province, which is now' paying $16.75, would continue to pay $16.75 as a supplement, making an adequate old age pension. The federal government would also

Old Age Pensions
pay half of the pensions down to age sixty-five, which is getting the old age pension age limit reduced. It is true they were to have a means test there. Of course there is a defence for the means test. If you have only so much money in the national budget to devote to old age pensions then you should certainly see that it goes to those who need it most which means the means test does. There is a counter-argument, of course, that if paid to everybody, the rich would give it back in income tax. That is a fallacious argument, because even in the very top branch of the income tax there is at least a twenty per cent amount kept by the income taxpayer and in the lower branches the actual amount kept would be three-quarters. That amount would be kept by people who do not really need it.
I would suggest that the exact standard used in the family allowances be adopted. An hon. member said there was no means test in family allowances. But there is a restriction on a sliding scale up to $3,000 on the amount of family allowance given. The argument is used that those who have incomes above that level do not need the help; but to avoid the taint of charity everyone is paid as of right. I would suggest that if the means test for pensions at sixty-five in the green book proposals should be adopted, or even, if by unfortunate chance the present bill should go ahead as it is, that the same thing should be done. The old age pension should be paid as of right, and returns secured by our present income tax exemption on a sliding scale. Hon. members will notice that the total allowable earnings, announced by the minister, of the pensioner come very close to the bottom income tax salary or wage. Therefore there would be very little change there. It would remove the taint of charity, and it would also facilitate the payments of old age pensions across the country, as is the case in family allowances. I think, too, that the government could well copy their own act, the War Veterans Allowances Act and pay the double pension, not just permit double the allowable outside earnings, if any, but double pension to any man or wife who, on reaching seventy years of age, has a spouse just below seventy. That would be copying their own good legislation.
Lastly, and I think most importantly, a start must be made on a contributory pension scheme. The simple way to do it is as they did it in the United States, expand our Unemployment Insurance Act. We have the administration already set up, and an expansion of the unemployment insurance with a slight increase in premium would begin a contributory scheme for all the industrial workers in
the country. The matter of finding funds then comes up. As has been pointed out by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), we must face up to it. Any scheme which is not contributory must be financed out of the public treasury which means payment of taxes.
I did not speak on the budget. I have spoken neither on the budget in the house nor on the radio to my constituents, because I had the feeling that it would have been a far better thing at this time to go ahead and enact an adequate old age pension scheme rather than provide tax cuts. It is quite true, of course, that both the Tories and the C.C.F. went after the government for not having made greater tax cuts, but at the same time ask for increased expenditures. Anybody who is paying income tax today is earning enough to live on. I do not think anyone in my riding, which is composed mostly of industrial workers, would have given great opposition to a lesser tax cut had they known that out of that revenue an adequate old age pension would be paid. For that reason I say that I cannot stand here and talk lower taxes and higher old age pensions. I believe in an adequate old age pension, and will forgo tax cuts to get it.
There is one last thing I should like to mention as a British Columbian. My province has been mentioned a great deal here in a congratulatory way. The remarks made by so many hon. members from the other eight provinces only go to show that they are envious of our record, for today everybody has been speaking very well of British Columbia. But the thought that is left in the minds of most members is that British Columbia is doing this because it is a rich province. British Columbia is rich in natural resources, but unlike Ontario and Quebec it has not been made rich by artificial laws, by the tariff, by exorbitant freight rates over the mountains, by the concentration of industries such as has taken place in Ontario and Quebec. Whatever riches we have we have got in the face of merciless competition from the central provinces, by being forced to buy our supplies in their protected markets and sell our goods on the open markets of the world. We have managed to keep ahead only by plundering our natural resources. Despite our difficult economic situation, the government out there has a remarkable appreciation of the plight of the old age pensioner. Of course we have many more old age pensioners per capita than any of the other provinces. There are two reasons for that. The first is the mild climate. An old age pensioner who is drawing $30 a month cannot afford to spend very much
Old Age Pensions

of that S30 on heating the room in which he is living, and so comes to British Columbia where a minimum of fuel is needed. The second reason is, of course, the fact that there is a higher pension paid there and old people are naturally attracted by this. That extra 85 is a very important $5 in the small amount paid to the old age pensioners. That is one reason w-hy I cannot understand why the British Columbia government has agreed, as the minister says, to this new way of apportioning the provincial costs. If an old age pensioner has lived for the greater part of three years immediately preceding application in the province where he applies, that province is now to take the total cost. I foresee British Columbia paying old age pension costs for the whole of western Canada if that goes through.
I must say my feeling is that a basic old age pension sufficient to secure an adequate standard of living across the whole country is a responsibility of the federal government. But I also say that a progressive local government which feels that it should, because of either local wealth or local need, supplement that pension, should be encouraged to do so. as we are doing in British Columbia.
I had thought that to stand up today and simply talk and give my views would not be of much help, because they are not so very different from the view's of most hon. members. The difficulty, however, of discussing old age pensions in this house is that w'e are speaking only with the facts and figures supplied from the government benches, and from those brain-trusters who are brought in to relay answers through the minister; but we have never had a good opportunity to take this legislation apart ourselves and to summon our own experts in a committee away from the committee of the whole.
It has been said in this house that no party has a monopoly on its interest in the problem of the old people. Unfortunately, however, the government has a monopoly on the preparation of legislation in that regard. My friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni came to me at noon today and suggested that perhaps we could do something about the matter. Instead of this bill being referred to the committee of the whole and the same vague sort of discussion being held again, this bill should be referred to the committee on industrial relations, where we could get before us some of the experts and question them ourselves. We could find out for ourselves exactly what it would cost the country to remove the means test, and what the constitutional difficulties are now in introducing a
contributory scheme, and what the attitude of the provinces is-

speechtext:
We are now' dealing with the second reading of a bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act. It brings into the act what has been done so far, including the start made in 1927 when the present government brought in the first old age pension scheme, as will be found in the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 156. By that act the dominion was to pay fifty per cent of the provincial expenditures. By an agreement with the provinces it was put on a fifty-fifty basis. By the revised statutes of 1931 that act was amended and the dominion increased its contribution from fifty per cent to seventy-five per cent of the provincial expenditures, and twenty-five per cent of the expenditures were carried by the provinces. By the statute of 1937 the blind, who should have been included long ago, were also added when they reached the age of over forty. I wish to state that, so far as I see it, the government have now gone seventy-five per cent of the way. They should go the whole way, because of the difficulties of this particular manner of doing business. I do not believe that it should be any part of politics. I do not believe that there is any room for party politics when we deal with so important a manner as care for the aged and afflicted. The problem is not political, but social only. After all, he that hath pity on the poor lendeth unto the Lord. The whole problem relates back to two important matters, overgovernment and overtaxation. We must remember that times have changed since the British North America Act of 1867, because there were no aeroplanes, no telephones, no radio and no automobiles when that act was passed. The development that has taken place in every direction since that time has resulted in

Old Age Pensions
overgovernment and overtaxation and waste in this country, and it is almost impossible for us now to deal with any social problem because of overlapping of jurisdiction and duplication of effort between the provinces and the dominion. The municipal system is an extension of the provincial system; in other words, we have one local system within another.
I should like to refer for a moment or two to the history of this question. When I first entered the House of Commons I pointed out, as I have pointed out many times since, that the larger municipalities of the country had instituted in the very early days of the century, in 1904. pensions for firemen, policemen, schoolteachers and others engaged in various services, on a contributory basis. As I say, however, owing to changed conditions it is impossible under the system we now have, and owing to the difficulties involved in the British North America Act, to deal properly in a contributory way with this problem. In the early days in Toronto we had a pension scheme, not contributory, whereby we paid $6 a week at the start and increased it to $12 for every employee over the age of sixty who was incapacitated or getting too old to carry on. In Toronto we have a local old age pension board, and I might say that the actual number of residents of our city receiving old age pensions in December of last year, the last year of record, was 11,425. They qualified under the act, and the amounts paid out totalled $3,672,000. At December 31, persons receiving blind pensions, paid to those over the age of forty, received $83,000. The city was required to provide office space for purposes of administration.
When I entered the House of Commons in 1922, I had a motion on the order paper with regard to this whole question of old age pensions. It was on the order paper the first day I came here, and in that motion I proposed that we should follow the system which had been followed in the old country, in France and elsewhere so as to give some direct aid to the aged by a modern system of old age pensions. Everywhere people were lodged in gaol or in homes of one description rnd another for no other reason than the fact tnat they were no longer able to make a living. They were too old to work. As every medical health officer will tell you, there is always a large part of the population who will be unable to work. There are about twenty-five per cent of the people who, from physical causes, find it impossible to earn a living. As I say. I introduced a resolution into the house in 1922, and Mr. Woodsworth, at one time a
member of this house, put on the order paper a similar motion a few months later. Both resolutions were referred to the industrial relations committee and that committee reported favourably to the House of Commons, but evidently the members at large were not prepared to support the proposal. There were a few votes for it on that occasion. This matter was referred to last year by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), who gave a fair statement of what had been done up to that time by Mr. Woodsworth and myself.
In 1927 the present government introduced the first legislation dealing with old age pensions. I suggest that the government should go much further than it has gone. In fact it should go the whole distance. It is contributing seventy-five per cent, and with such economy as could be effected in the administration of other departments it might very well go the whole way. The minister has made a considerable extension under this bill. In 1940 the government's contribution was $29,141.000. Of course a stupendous war was on and not much could be done, but in 1941 the amount was $28,472,000; in 1942, $28,770,000; in 1943. $30,496,000. Then they brought in the blind. In 1944 it was something like $38,000.000 and in 1945 the amount was $40,722,000. Now it is $60,000,000 and, if I understood the minister's speech correctly', this year's bill is not final; it will go eventually to nearly' $100,000,000.
So far so good, but one of the objections I have to this way' of looking after the problem is the means test. I am opposed to it. It is well named when it is called the "means test". I know a family in Toronto with five children. The father died, having been unable to work for years, and, he had been getting an old age pension of a total over the years of $472. After he had died they billed his estate, which was worth very little, if anything, apart from a small house, because this means test had to be applied.
Some provision should be made in these grants to take care of the high cost of living, because today a room costs more than the amount of the pension for one person. You have to pay the amount received by the pensioner. $28 or $29 or $30 a month, and sometimes it is almost impossible to get a room for that amount.
The blind were brought into this scheme and throughout the provinces, from Prince Edward Island to British Columbia, there is an average of 824 per person. I suggest that special consideration shou'd, be given the blind
Old Age Pensions

because they must have a guide, and they have to meet other expenses that persons not so afflicted do not incur.
I hope that in the recess of parliament some study will be made of this problem. The government should canvass the whole situation and we should have a national system of old age pensions, because that is the only way in which we can properly deal with the problem. The day has long gone by when it should be made a political football, something peculiar to the party system-"You did this; we did that", and all that kind of thing. Where do the poor people come in in the meantime? "Faith without works is dead."
Another objection to the system is, I think, the residence provision of twenty years in the country and the five-year residence rule in the provinces. That rule should be amended, because twenty years is altogether too long to qualify for a $30 pension. I hope there will be some improvement in the law. The government should make it a national responsibility and' take it over from the provinces. Even if you pass this bill, you will have to make agreements tomorrow with the provinces, and that will take months, so that probably next winter no one will qualify to gain anything under the legislation.
Mr. ANG'US MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): Several members prefaced' their remarks in this debate by saying that no party had any monopoly of the concern for the welfare of our senior citizens, as the phrase has been used. I am quite willing to agree to that without any reservation. I have a particular interest in this matter myself because, among our group, as I suppose among all parties in this house, we try to have our members specialize in the things in which they are most interested or for the consideration of which they are best fitted. In the arrangement of work the matter of old age pensions was allotted to me. In the last two sessions I introduced resolutions urging this House of Commons to give an expression of opinion on the Old Age . Pensions Act. On both occasions I asked for three changes in the act: reduction in the age, an increase in the amount of the pension, and removal of the means test. This afternoon I shall try to confine myself to urging upon the government that they take further action in those three vital matters.
Yesterday the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) asked the leader of this party, just as he was concluding his speech, if we were opposed to the improvements in the Old Age Pensions Act amendment which

is now before us. That is an old political catch question. I want to reply to it right away and say that we will not vote against this bill as it is, although we consider it shamefully inadequate. I think the storm which the introduction of this bill has raised in this house, and what has been said on both sides, should be sufficient proof to the government that the measure they have introduced meets with the approval, neither of members of this house, nor of the people of this country.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) spoke a little while ago, he said he favoured a contributory form of old age pension, so that the pensioner would get his pension as of right and not as a charity. Surely the minister did not want to imply that the pension now is a form of charity. Even as a form of charity it is inadequate. But for my present purposes I do not care whether it is on a contributory basis or whether it is paid out of the consolidated revenue funds of the federal and provincial governments. I contend that it is not now charity and cannot be defined as such. By and large, the people who receive monetary benefits under this scheme have earned their right to them because of their contribution as citizens of the country, and I object to any attempt to place it on the basis of charity.
The first point I shall deal with is the amount of the pension. When introducing the measure yesterday, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) said that this was in effect an increase of $10 a month.

speechtext:
Yes. I believe they could. They would not have a very good living. I want to assure him that they could not live as well as he and I can live. Nevertheless I believe they could get by. But I do not think they can get by on $30 a month.
I know a great deal is made of the fact that the amount of income pensioners can have, over and above the pension, has been increased, and I am grateful that has been done. But those who receive benefits under this bill fall into two categories, namely, those who depend on the pension for their entire living, and those who have other income with which to supplement the pensions. The minister has said that they cannot live on $30 a month and that they cannot live on even $50 a month. I think there is general agreement that no individual in Canada can live on $30 a month and that if they are compelled to try to exist on that amount, it just means slow starvation. In this rich country, where we have demonstrated that we can produce so abundantly, I am of the opinion that no one should be asked to live on an income which means ultimate starvation.
Let us look at the situation as it really is. I obtained cost of living figures today from the bureau of statistics. Taking the cost of living index of 1935-39 as 100, as at May 1 of this year the cost of living index was 133-1. That was the general cost of living index. That is an increase of one-third in the cost of living since 1939. One-third of $30 is $10; and with the addition of this $10 the old age pensioner is where he was in 1939. In my own opinion he is even worse off, because the cost of living index for food, which was 100 for the period from 1935 to 1939, was 154-9 or 155 on May 1 of this year. Since those in the low income brackets spend a greater percentage of their income on food than those receiving larger incomes, consequently the $30 received by the old age pensioner is worth considerably less than it was in 1939.

So we can say that under this measure we are not really holding our own. It reminds me of those folk in "Alice in Wonderland" who had to run with all their might to remain in the same place. Here we are doing exactly what we have been doing all along the line by our reductions in income tax, the elimination of subsidies and so on. We are helping those who have something already and taking away from those who have not, even the little they have. So I would suggest to the minister and the government that the proposal made by this party early this winter, of $50 a month, is not a bit too high.
The next point I want to touch upon is the eligible age. When the Old Age Pensions Act was passed in 1927 the eligible age was set at seventy. I could never understand why it was done. I have a suspicion, realizing the familiarity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with scripture, that it was because in the ninetieth psalm it says the age of a man is three score years and ten, and they decided that if they made the age seventy, which is three twenties and ten, and made the pension $20, it would not cost the government much anyway as no one could live very long on that amount. And we are still sticking to it. I do not wish to bring into this debate any invidious comparisons as between what Canada is doing and what other countries are doing in this regard, but I will make a few comparisons. I should like, before doing that, to quote from the proposals of the dominion government to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction in August, 1945. On page 37 and other pages of this document considerable space is given to old age pensions, and I am going to quote briefly from those proposals because they express the opinion of this government at that time..
Today the question was asked as to whether Saskatchewan would now increase its supplementary contribution to equal that of British Columbia and Ontario. That question is one of those political catch-phrases that should not be used at a time like this. You might ask the same thing in regard to Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick or Nova
Old Age Pensions

Scotia or one or two other provinces. Some provinces in Canada can increase the amount of pension above S30 a month, but there are other provinces which, no matter how much they might desire to do so, cannot because of their limited financial resources. In the proposals made by the federal government to the conference in 1945 that fact was recognized. They said:
Thus, in one province 28 per cent of all persons age 70 and over were receiving old age pensions in 1945, and in another province 57 per cent. Likewise, the amount of average monthly pension varies from $18.63, in one province to $29.41 (including provincial supplement) in another.
Then I want the minister to pay particular attention to this:
Generally speaking, the need for pensions is, as might be expected, greatest in those provinces which are least able to finance such payments out of local revenues.
What is the use of all the tommyrot, asking is this province going to do this, or is it going to do that? As I have pointed out, several provinces, no matter how much they may want to increase the pension, cannot possibly do so, as the minister knows very well.

Well, I don't know: I
realize that it affects your effectiveness as an opposition member, but during my time in this house I have tried not to ask the government. to do anything I would not be prepared to do myself if I were in the place of the government. So now when I ask the government to increase the pension to $50 a month, I am asking them to do something I would do if I were in the government; and if it were not done I would walk out of the government. I will now put on record some of the government's own policies in regard to old age pensions, as presented to the dominion-provincial conference in 1945. The section to which I am referring is entitled "Deficiencies of the present scheme," and may I say this bill has removed very few of those deficiencies:
(1)	The means test is generally recognized as undesirable after a certain age. It has been noted that about 40 per cent of all persons of seventy years of age and over make application, satisfy the means test requirements, and receive pensions.
That is, forty per cent under the Old Age Pension Act as it is at the present time, which demands almost absolute destitution for qualification. Forty per cent of the people reaching the age of seventy years in this country, who make application for old age pension, satisfy the means test requirements and receive the pension. I say that does not speak well for the fairness of the distribution of wealth in this country. Then it goes on:
There is little doubt that a very considerable number in addition are not able entirely to support themselves but are dependent upon their family and refrain from applying for pensions because of the embarrassment occasioned by the means test.
If you have not there all the arguments necessary for the removal of the means test, particularly after the age of sixty-five, then I do not know what other evidence can be produced. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, it is the government's own statement. Then:
(2)	The minimum age of 70 though convenient as a dividing line with respect to the payment of any kind of universal old age pension, is nevertheless too high in a number of cases of actual need. A strong case can be made for reducing the age limit to 65 in order to provide assistance at least for those in the age group 65 to 69 who are actually in need.
(3)	The statutory amount of $20 per month, although increased to $25 during the war, may still be too low as a national minimum.
That is an understatement, if I ever heard one.

Old Age Pensions
(4)	Any broad extension of the present plan would impose serious burdens on limited local revenues in a number of provinces. Even without such an extension, the costs will increase very considerably as the proportion of old persons in the population will continue to rise for 30 or 40 years.
In view of that, I ask this question: How can the government bring down a measure of this kind without a substantial increase in the amount of pension, and without a substantial reduction, if I may use that term, in the eligible age?
As I said before, I do not wish to make comparisons. I do not indeed want to say anything that would give my remarks any partisan or political connotation. But I must point out that, so far as I know, there is no other country, comparable in wealth with ours, which has an eligible age as high as ours, an eligible age of seventy years. In Great Britain the age is sixty for women and sixty-five for men. In New Zealand it is sixty for both men and women, and in Australia it is the same.
A person could go on for an hour giving reason after reason why the eligible age should be reduced at least from seventy to sixty-five.

speechtext:
When the house took recess at six o'clock we were discussing the bill on old age pensions which had been brought down yesterday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I cannot think of any piece of legislation this session that could mean any more or be any more important perhaps than legislation on old age pensions. I do not suppose that I ever visit any part of my constituency without having someone come to me and ask what is being done on behalf of our aged citizens. We are all asked such questions as:	When will the pension be
raised? When will the age limit be reduced? And what answers have we been able to give? Over the past few months, and particularly since the session opened and the speech from the throne was read, hopes were raised. At last the long expected has happened. The bill has arrived. I do not want to be considered too harsh this evening in my criticism; but I will say that the forty or fifty-minute speech which the minister made when he

Old Age Pensions
introduced the bill amounted to nothing more or less than an apology for a poor job badly done.
I cannot imagine how it is that, with all the wealth of our country, all that we are able to do is to increase the old age pensions by around $5 a month. We live in perhaps the wealthiest country in the world in respect of natural wealth and productivity, and yet all we can do is to give our aged people the barest necessities of life. With our abundant wealth we can keep the wolf only from coming too far inside the door.
In his speech the minister made a great deal of the Liberal government's desire for social security. He referred to the present Liberal leadership and carried us back over the years in an attempt to show the gradual growth of their social service programme. Then he projected the house into the future in another attempt to show how the present administration has worked toward contributory social services, including a scheme for contributory old age pension. The alarming thing to me is that, when he said that, he also told us that fifty per cent of our aged people are on old age pensions.
The present administration have been at the helm for a good many years. It has been their responsibility so to legislate and so to administer the affairs of this country that people should be able to have security in their old c.ge, and yet the same administration of which the minister boasted so much find themselves in a position -where fifty per cent of our aged people have not been able to make life secure and contented for themselves. I wonder whether the minister is proud of that.
In talking of a contributory old age pension scheme which he hoped the present government might be able to introduce at some time-he did not say when; perhaps when I am a very old man-the minister said that if the government went too far in giving to our aged citizens too large a pension scheme it might have the result of throwing everything out of balance when the time came to put in a contributory scheme. That is tantamount to saying to our aged, "We are sorry we cannot give you more because when we eventually ask our younger citizens to pay for their security when they are old they will revolt and say, why do we have to pay for this? Our mothers and fathers have all the security they want, and they did not have to pay for it." The minister might just as well have said that. When he made those remarks he emphasized with great tenderness, .if you please, that he was saying it with the greatest
respect. I said I did not want to be too harsh, but I say to the minister as kindly as I can that he said it with the greatest disrespect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government want to move on from the present old age pension scheme, which is non-contributory, to a pension scheme which is contributory. In other words, they want to move from the present taxation scheme to another type of taxation scheme in order to pay them that pension. At the present time we are all taxed to pay the aged. That is nothing more or less than a form of charity. When we tax the people themselves under a contributory scheme, so that by that taxation they put aside something for themselves in their declining years, then we chisel on their present incomes. So that, what the government desire to do is to move from the principle of charity to a principle of chiselling.
Surely the citizens of this country have what might be called a common heritage. Here we are living in a very modern civilization when we can produce so much because of our scientific power age. Who is it that supplied that science and that power? Was it the present generation? Why, of course not. Throughout the centuries of time, civilization developed, one generation built upon another, and the reason we live in this modern age is that our forefathers long since left, us a common heritage. Surely it is not just to say that the only people who can inherit that common heritage are those who have invested their dollars; in other words, it is not just for that common heritage to go only to those who happen to have the monetary units that have come their way.
The minister gave a great number of figures and a great deal of statistics. His speech seemed to be loaded with figures and statistics. And what was it all for? It was all for the purpose of trying to impress the country with the idea that the government could not afford to pay any higher pensions. We cannot afford to do it! I wonder what that phrase means. I said we had come along through the centuries of. time to a very high order of civilization. Let us go back over the centuries and see what sort of civilization they used to have, and we can go back to the cave men if we want to.
I imagine the cave men are holding their council meeting and the chief of the council says: "Gentlemen, we have a younger generation coming along; our population is increasing; it is necessary for us to establish another community just across the river. Let us discuss the question how we < an establish that
Old Age Pensions

community. Have we enough stone in the vicinity? Have we enough lumber? Have we enough human skill in our tribe?" Through the council of these cave men they decide: "Yes; we have the stone; we have the timber; we have the human skill". In other words, they decide that it is physically possible to do it.
Now imagine some jmunger man of the council rising in his place. I do not suppose this younger man was from the constituency of Essex East; I do not suppose he was the minister of health and welfare in the tribe. But suppose some young chap in the council should rise and say: "Mr. Chieftain, may I have a word? It is true we have the stone and the timber, the man-power and the skill; but. Mr. Chieftain, do you think we can afford it?"
I think the chieftain would look at that young man and say: "Young man, are you not feeling very well?" Now, if we have come so far in bur modern civilization, if we have developed so much in our modern way of living, have we become so confounded with our science that we are behind the men of the stone age? They did what to them was physically possible, but even though it be physically possible for us to produce an abundance and to distribute it to all, the minister rises in his place and says, "Yes; it is physically possible but we cannot afford it." I feel like asking him if he is not feeling very well. Yet he is the minister of health. He should be feeling all right.
It is true, is it not, that the present Liberal administration of this country have the power to do three things. They have the power to legislate; they have the power to tax- and believe me they have been exercising that power-and they have the power to create the means of payment out of nothing, the way our present banking system is doing it today. They have all three powers, and yet they say they cannot afford to increase the old age pension. What do they mean? Do they mean that they cannot afford to create the means of payment? Do they mean that they cannot afford to create those monetary symbols we call dollars, which is only another name given to figures used for a certain purpose?
Suppose this country wanted a road somewhere and the minister should rise in his place and say, "Well, yes, we would like to have that road. WTe have the gravel, the machinery and the man-power, but we cannot ouild the road because we have not enough miles". Then we would surely ask him if he was not feeling very well. But he might just as well say that we cannot build the road
because we have no miles as to say that we cannot increase old age pensions because we have no figures. That is the truth of the matter. They have the power to legislate. They have the power to tax if they wish to, and we do not believe they have to tax to do it; they have the power over currency and credit.

It was published by the national Liberal committee. The address is not given but it emanated from the Liberal headquarters in Canada. It is entitled "Just Plain Sense". speechtext:
Yes, that is Liberal
politics, when they raise the hopes of our aged mothers and fathers and then dash them to pieces when they bring down the bill. The very word "pension" means that a person is given a certain security for life. The word "pension" does not carry with it any idea of charity. The very moment the means test is brought into the old age pensions scheme, it is reduced from a pension to charity. As soon as the factor of financial

status comes into the picture, the whole character of the plan is altered. It is not a pensions scheme at all then. It is nothing more or less than glorified charity which is imposed upon our aged parents by a system of beggary. Our aged mothers and fathers do not mind proving their age. Some of them are proud of the honour. Some of our aged people are revered. We respect them. One of the first Christian principles is respect for the aged. When they apply for old age pensions, they are quite willing to prove that they were born on a certain day and that they have now reached pensionable age. It is not humiliating for them to prove their age. But they must not only prove their age; they must prove their poverty. Furthermore, because of existing regulations, they must prove that they will continue to be paupers. I want to ask if that is a respectable old age pension scheme. Surely when a pensions act is brought down, it should be brought down with dignity for our aged people. Surely we should say to our aged people, "You have lived well. You have pioneered this country. We now give to you part of your heritage as a right of citizenship. We give you the reward .for being respectable citizens."
There is something else which should be involved in any pension scheme. Any government or any treasury board should administer a pension scheme with this one great principle in mind: we are now giving it to you and we want to give you more. But what has happened through all the regulations we have had in our pensions bills? We have had regulations which have made inspectors nothing more or less than white-collared sleuths going around to see whether or not our aged parents earned a dollar.

speechtext: Our aged parents cannot earn a dollar without having the bloodhounds on their tracks. Parliament passes legislation for the purpose of providing pensions. That, shall I say, should be our objective. But the government comes along and makes such regulations that, in effect, they take upon themselves to do their best to prevent our aged people from getting the full pension. That is what actually happens in practice. I said that pensions as administered today and as administered under this new bill are a form of charity. Our aged people have to prove their povert3r. Let me ask one question. Why is an aged person poor in this country? Here is one thing I should like to say at the very start. As I used to go around in those depression days-and I do not want to refer to that too much-how often hive I heard this remark, "Oh, well, that man has not got anything because he was not thrifty enough; he did not save enough."

speechtext: Yes; that he was too lazy to work, and so on and so forth. Thrift was regarded as a sort of virtue. Let me say that it is time we were revising our thinking. In these days the term "thrift" has become perverted. We formerly used it in the sense that mother would sew patches on our trousers; she would save materials, and put away foodstuffs so that they would not spoil. Why? Because in an age of scarcity people had to practise thrift. But in a modern civilization thrift has become nothing but a pinch-penny business of never spending. How are the wheels of industry made to go around? By people spending. I want to say, with the greatest respect, that a good citizen is one who will spend his money. It is a poor citizen who will save his money, strange as that may sound, because you cannot save money and at the same time turn the wheels of industry.

You see this is an asinine system under which we are living. A man has to save or he will not have anything; yet the more men save, the less our ultimate production becomes, and the less we get. It is all back end forward, and the present administration evidently have not the wisdom to
Old Age Pensions

put the right end forward. The same thing goes for contributory pensions, which simply mean that money is taken out of the stream of purchasing power. We need to recognize that we have passed that pinch-penny phase of finance, and that we now live in an age of abundance.
I should like to refer to one or two other matters before my time speeds away. There is another disappointment which will be sad for our aged people; that is, that there is no reduction in the age limit. They were hoping that something along this line would be done. I can quite understand the government not being able to give us all the details and facts and figures of their pension scheme ahead of time, but at least they could have said something like this:	"We will raise the old age
pension, we will not say how much, but we will not lower the age limit." Then our aged people would have known what would happen. But that is not the picture; the picture is that our aged people were living in hope that the age limit would be lowered. Why did the government not come out and say, "We want you aged people to know you cannot expect the age limit to be lowered at the present time," instead of raising their hopes and then dashing them on the rocks of disappointment?
I should like to mention a few other things with respect to pensions, but I shall touch upon them only in passing. There is a class of people in this country who are entirely forgotten. I mentioned this last year; I shall mention it again now. I refer to those people who are numbered among the incurables. This does not, I know, come directly under old age pensions, but here are young men and young women who have been struck down by infantile paralysis, epilepsy, and so on. They are bed-ridden cases, pronounced absolutely incurable, and are thrown upon charity for the rest of their lives. In a land of abundance, a land of wealth, a land where we are short of nothing, we cannot look after them. I wish some Liberal member would explain why that should be. The only explanation they can give is: "We have not the money."

I said once in the house that I had no hope of getting to the senate because there are too many ahead of me. Probably there are some priorities in the matter.
The present means test of course places the stigma of pauperdom on anyone who applies for an old age pension, when one considers the investigations which take place, and to which reference has already been made in the house. I believe I can honestly say that there is no
Old Age Pensions

member in the House of Commons but who, because of the amount of expenses members have, will find a great deal of difficulty in making both ends meet, despite the raise of $2,000 we got last year. I do not believe there is a member in the House of Commons who would care to go to the old age pensions authority and ask for a pension for his mother or father. In my view that condition of affairs is wrong. If wre have an old age pension it should be available to every old person, and should not be payable by the children, even if they are able to pay it. Under the means test, the present pension is a form of charity, in the way it is administered.
I object very much to the fact that people who have been thrifty and who have provided for their old age find that, when examinations are made, their pensions are cut in half in some cases. There is no provision made for people of that kind, who have saved, to obtain a cost of living bonus. They certainly are not organized today, like members of labour unions, so that, because of the present high cost of living, they might be able to obtain some relief.
I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) to refer the bill to the committee on industrial relations is a good one; and I can see no reason, if the government were prepared to support that suggestion, why there should be any necessity to have this bill killed. There is no reason why we cannot go ahead with this old age pensions bill in this session of parliament. It seems to me that the average responsible member in the House of Commons would like to know what the removal of the means test would cost.

. Mr. McIVOR: -I note the contrast in these views. I believe this bill has come a long way in doing good. I was only sorry that this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that, on account of the bill, the minister should bow his head in shame. My experience in life is that no man should bow his head in shame unless he commits a sin. I believe the minister should hold his head higher because of what he has done in the bill for people who are in difficulties. I am pleased with the amendments that have been brought in, and there is one that I appreciate very much. I know of many people who moved from the country during the war, some going to the south and some to the old country. When they could not get back they lost their pensions because they had stayed away for more than the allotted number of days. They are now to be able to get their pensions and I thank the minister for that.
I notice that there is to be a fifty-fifty payment to those between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine years who are in difficulties financially. That is a good thing because some men are older at sixty-five than others are at seventy-five. I have no difficulty in proving that. Some men hold their youth because thej- take care of themselves; some do not

Old Age Pensions
because they do not take care of their minds. I thank the minister for that fifty-fifty payment.
I have heard some say that it is too little and too late. There were a lot of people in this house who said that the war effort of this government was too little and too late. I must admit that it went down below my diaphram when I heard that, because I thought we were not doing all that we could. What happened? The government was doing everything behind the scenes to help Britain and Russia defeat Hitler. It was not too little and too late because they won out in the end.
I want to tell the minister that I think he is on the right track. It may not be a large pension, but it is something. I know a couple whom I helped get an old age pension, and they are now each receiving $28 a month, or a total of S56. I had pancakes and coffee with them in their home and anyone would have been glad to have had a meal like that. Everything was clean and tidy and they were saving a little for their old age. They showed me their bank book.
I have used the words of that great Scottish poet because he understood human nature. I want to congratulate Ontario-there are some here representing that province-upon raising its old age pension to $40 a month. My hon. friends from British Columbia must now take second place to our great province. I want to thank that province for its generosity; I want to give credit where credit is due. There will be some people who are sufficiently hard-hearted to say that that is smart politics. If it is, let us have more politics of that kind because it will help many older people get their S40 a month. I believe the minister is indirectly responsible for that increase.
What is going to happen in Quebec, and I dare to refer to your great province, Mr. Speaker? I do not think Quebec will take second place to Ontario or British Columbia. I did not meet him there, but I see the premier of Quebec is attending the great Marian congress. If he gets the spirit of that congress there will be nobody in want in Quebec. He will go back to his cabinet and say, "We as a great province cannot stand idly by and not feed and clothe our old people, not give them a bit of fun and a little :obacco into the bargain."
There are some people who think members of parliament are paid a lot of money, and dear knows we are. However I am no richer today than I was ten years ago. The more we get, the more we spend and we are the happier at it. I would be glad to have my sessional indemnity held by the government if it would
increase old age pensions a little or help those who are suffering from arthritis or who cannot get treatment when they are suffering from cancer.
There is another side to this great question. When I was quite young I was taught to memorize the ten commandments, and there is one commandment I have never forgotten: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee." I do not think any young man or woman should take the farm or property of his or her parents, have it put in his or her name and then let the old folks go on old age pensions. It is not fair to the government.
There is another thing in this bill I like very much, the possibility of a national pensions scheme. The minister made it quite clear that we should have contributory pensions. Those who have worked in our day remember that there were many who earned fifty cents an hour but when the week was over they did not have a cent left. They had not the ability or willingness to save a little. If there were a contributory scheme on a national basis it would be a great thing for this country. I say to the minister, more power to your arm and to your head for your willingness to keep this thing going.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) congratulated the minister upon piloting the citizenship bill through the house. I am not an Irishman, nor is the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) a Scotsman; we are both Canadians and we thank the minister for that. I know, when the minister tackles this question of pensions for our senior citizens it will be like the balky horse I helped to break in. When he once got the bit in his mouth he would go his own way, no matter what any one did. I hope the minister gets the bit in his mouth and goes to the finish. As I said before, we shall not then be giving our older citizens $50 a month, we shall be giving them enough, no matter what the standard of living is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that nothing I say shall be interpreted as politics. To my mind politics should be left out of this subject. The distress of old folks should not be played up politically.
In the addresses so far in the debate, there is one matter that has not been touched upon. Most of those now coming into the old age pension brackets are those who have come down through the years without large wages or salaries. Something has been said about the large salaries and wages which have been
Old Age Pensions

paid in late years, but that does not apply to those now coming up for old age pensions.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) spoke this afternoon he referred to the length of time he had been advocating old age pensions. My advocacy of old age pensions and pensions for the maimed and blind goes back to some years prior to 1920. I became an enthusiast of pensions for the blind and for the maimed and aged workers from a long association with thousands of workers. Many times I saw them blinded and maimed. I saw thousands of them getting old. I am talking of the time when I was with them. I know these men with whom I worked, and multitudes of others now coming into the old age pension age down through the years who did not at any time receive * sufficient salary or wage to lay up a competence for their old age I think of the moulders, of the machinists, and of the artificers working in a big plant of whom I knew so many. I saw them laid off quite often for as much as three months of the year. A man cannot save very much for his old age if he is laid off work for three months of the year. I am not speaking of the last ten years because everything has been swimming in that time. I am speaking of the time years before that, of the people who are now coming into the old age pension age. Being working men, most of them had families. God blesses the working man. It is to those people that He sends the families. Many of their wives were frequently sick. If a man is out of work and has sickness in his home he cannot save at all. Therefore, sir, I am one of those who advocates as strongly as I can the abolition of the means test. That is my own opinion. I do not care a fig about what anybody else advocates. I give my own opinion and my opinions are based on my experience. We should abolish the means test. How in the name of heaven could a moulder, a blacksmith, a machinist or a carpenter fifteen or twenty years ago, out of the mere pittance of a salary or wage that he received, lay aside anything for his old age? They did manage to get together a little home. How in the name of common sense can we ask them, when they ask for old age pension after the struggle of a lifetime, to sign away the rights to their little homes?
I hold in my hand a letter which I received from a lady I know in Toronto. Her husband was a soldier. He went overseas in the first great war. He was not allowed to go to France because he was too proficient at drilling or in some other army service. He was an expert in that line and they kept him in 
England. When he came back to Canada he died. That service barred him from a military pension and also his wife. But through thrift they had managed to get together a little home. I know the home very well. It may be worth $2,500. I am not speaking of the inflated prices of houses today which will certainly be flattened out in the next few years. As I say, that house is worth $2,500, but it would probably sell at S7,500 today. She came to see me and importuned to get an old age pension, but she had to sign away her home. At that time her son, who was a returned soldier, was living with her. After a while he died and left her in straitened circumstances. She decided to sell her home because she could not possibly live on $20 a month and whatever was given in pension by Ontario plus the cost of living allowance. She sold her house after having received a pension for just a few years. Of course the old age pension board was at once notified about the sale of the house and they took from what she had received for the house all that they had paid her in old age pension; so she came to see me again. She has now bought a much smaller house for which she paid around $2,200. but it is not nearly as fine a house as the one she sold, because the one she bought recently was built recently and everyone knows what kind of houses they are.
She applied for old age pension again because she could not live on what was coming in from the little bit that she had left after selling her house. An old age pension official came to see her. I had appealed to the department to give this war widow of seventy-seven or seventy-eight years of age a chance to live. They wanted her to sign a paper for this little house worth about $2,200. I said to her: "Do not sign it." I am bound to say that she did receive old age pension this time without having to sign away her house. Whether it was a special ruling or not, I do not know. Anyway, she was given a pension without a means test. The means test should be abolished.
Some time ago I received a letter from her. I will not give her name. The letter reads:
I have had a note from the old age pension board to say they would reinstate me-
This is a month or two ago now. I continue:
-but they gave me no assurance that the same thing won't be repeated. They asked me to sign. I did not, as I don't trust them again.
I cannot blame her for that after her other experience. The letter continues:
It is too bad they can only gyp old people and poor widows who are left alone. I do think the thrifty people should be considered a little more

Old Age Pensions
after paying taxes fifty years and not penalize them for being thrifty and clean. 1 for one think it is a detriment to the housing shortage as people will not buy on account of that. I am sending you two more victims I cut out of the Telegram this week.
She sent me two items from the paper about two more people who had been victimized by their homes. Because of the numbers of experiences I have come in contact with, I am opposed to the means test. However I am glad to say that it has not been 100 per cent enforced. I know of two or three cases myself where the head of the hous<5 died; then the mother died; and the old age pension board in settling up with the estate, after my writing them a letter and telling them that one family had sent seven sons overseas-the parents had left nothing but the little home they had saved up-did not take the home away from the heir. While some lose their homes, others do not. I think it would be only fair all round to abolish the means test.
I know quite well that some people do not always do the right thing. They will sign away their homes to their children in order to get a pension without signing. A farmer will sign away his farm to his son or daughter in order to get a pension without signing. I do not think people should be put in the position of falsifying their financial status. It would be much better simply to abolish the means test.
