speechtext:
I had a letter a day or two ago from a clergyman's widow; she is one of a multitude I know. She is getting up toward seventy years of age. Her husband had been a clergyman in a charge in Saskatchewan or Alberta. Anyone who knows anything about the salaries of clergymen in the west a few years ago knows that they could not save anything out of their salary. Before going to the first great war, he was invited to take some official position in the army which did not allow him to get a pension. He came home and died. That poor widow woman of sixty-five years of age or more cannot even buy car tickets; she cannot buy any clothes; she cannot go to a picture show. She lives in one room with another family. She has nothing for medicine; she cannot have her teeth attended to. She has nothing that makes life worth living. She is just living to be taken away to the next world. That is not a situation of which any of us can be proud. Therefore I am in favour of lowering the age 83166-281
limit to permit women, perhaps especially widowed mothers, to receive pensions at the age of sixty-five.
I know that this or any other government would have a stiff job providing pensions for everyone at the age of sixty-five. I am not one of those who advocate high taxes, but I believe in lowering the age limit for women to sixty-five, because, after all, women age more rapidly than men, particularly if they have, had families. That is the position I take, and one of the reasons I take it is that during the years I served in big industry, coming into contact with thousands of workers in my time, I have seen too many of them going down the years unable to put by anything against their old age.
I am strongly in favour of lowering, the age limit, for women in particular to sixty-five, and I also strongly advocate the abolition of the means test. I do not wish to say a word that would inject politics into this debate. Someone tried to do so earlier in the evening, but this is not a debate for politics. If, therefore, I say that I am very happy that the Ontario government has made the announcement it has, I hope no one will interpret that observation as political. The sum of $40 a month by the Ontario premier will cheer the heart and soul of many old folks in this province.
That brings this thought to my mind, and I am sure it will be shared by the minister, for he is just as much interested in these matters as any other member of this house, and perhaps more, considering that he is minister. I hope it will be an incentive to him, if not this year, then perhaps next year, to try to bring about uniformity throughout Canada. Forty dollars at least for every province would be an objective to aim at, because if we get it in Ontario and the people do not get more than $32 or $33 or $35, say in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick or elsewhere, that is a penalty imposed on them for living in those provinces. That is not fair. The amount should be uniform throughout Canada, and I hope the minister will look ahead to some time in the near future when the rate will be the same. throughout the dominion. I am well aware of the fact that Viscount Bennett did announce that the federal government would pay the whole pension, and I believe I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) say that that had been in the Liberal platform. So there is no politics in my saying that, and I think that is the way it should be, that the federal government should carry the whole burden of the old age pension. After all, it goes round and round and it all comes back anyway. We get it in

Old Age Pensions

the form of sales tax or one tax or another, so that in reality it all comes out of the pocket of the federal government in any event.
I do not know that I have much more to say.
I have taken an interest in the old age pension question for many years. I do not take my hat off to anyone in the advocacy of it, for I advocated it as a necessity many years ago for those I knew so well. I do not think it is necessary for me to go further. I do not wish to criticize, because that will not get us anywhere. On the contrary, I would encourage the minister to go still farther, and if what I have said will help him to do so, when the bill comes in the committee it may be that, after consultation with his colleagues, amendments will be offered for the abolition of the means test or lowering the age limit, for instance. I hope someone will move an amendment to that effect and also propose that there be uniformity throughout Canada in the way I have suggested. If anything I have said will help the minister to go farther I feel that I have done my duty. I put my duty first to those who are in the class requiring old age pensions, and if I interject politics into the question I know it will do no good. It will not help either us or those who are in need of old age pensions.
Mr.' F. S. ZAPLITNY (Dauphin): In discussing this measure, which is an act to amend the Old Age Pensions Act, I believe that we in this house should be careful not to become too deeply involved in dollars and cents. The question of how it will be paid for is, I think, a minor consideration compared with the question whether it is desirable or not that we shall have better pensions and at a lower age. It seems to me that what we need to do first is to set out for ourselves what are the desirable national objectives and then try to introduce measures in this house in order to make them possible. Everyone will agree that if we were to state our national objectives in a brief way we would desire, first of all, that the general welfare of all citizens shall be looked after. We would strive for the highest possible standard of public health and also the highest possible standard of education.
What we are debating at the present time is not the desirability of these things, because I believe that we can agree on them. We are debating, however, whether the present government and the measure which is at present before us are adequate toward attaining these desirable ends. If we take the speech delivered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) yesterday, and consider two parts of it together, it will give us

a lead as to whether the government, in this measure, is reaching out far enough to attain these desirable objectives.
First, I wish to quote from the minister's speech where he referred to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on a different occasion, and which incidentally I placed on Hansard on a previous day, having to do with what the Prime Minister declared in 1942, on October 9, speaking to the American Federation of Labour in Toronto. He said:
The era of freedom will be achieved only as social security and human welfare 'become the main concern of men and nations.
He followed that up with this significant sentence:
It is necessary that social security and human welfare should be expressed in definite terms.
I come back to the earlier part of the minister's speech in which he said, at page 4282 of Hansard:
This government has given conclusive evidence of its concern for the welfare of the aged among our population.
I do not know what he meant by "conclusive evidence", but I would take it that the present measure is the conclusive evidence to which he referred of the extent to which the government is expressing its concern for the aged of the country.

speechtext:
What we have before the house is the present bill, and we have to decide on the basis of its provisions whether the government is expressing its concern for the aged and to what extent in definite terms, using the language of the Prime Minister. This is the measure that is before the house. I hope the proposals made to the provinces will be repeated in definite terms in the form of a bill in this house at a future time, but at the present time this bill is all that we have before us, and on that basis I fear I must agree with those on this side of the house who have expressed disappointment and criticism of the method, not only for the meagreness of the provision under consideration, but also for the fact that the measure has been so long delayed.
I want to agree with something that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said this

Old Age Pensions
evening. He observed that when we consider such measures as social security and other desirable objectives we should ask ourselves whether it is physically possible to provide the goods and services that are required before we get into any question of finance; because if we decide that it is desirable to have old age pensions at the age of sixty-five and at the rate of S50 a month, and if we have the natural resources and the productivity to provide the goods and services therefor, then the only question that remains to be decided is whether we shall divert the necessary portion of our production to provide for those people, or whether we shall not.
I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) came out pretty plainly and flat-footedlv when he said that it would be possible to provide for these people, that we could build them an hotel as good as the Chateau Laurier and bring meals to their rooms, but he asked, who is going to pay for it? So you see, we are not prepared to do these things for the aged people. We can do them but we are not prepared to do them. He does not think it would be fair for the other people to provide such facilities. I am not advocating that we build any hotels for our aged people, but I say that the people of this country have expressed in no uncertain terms their belief that people at the age of sixty-five are entitled to a pension of $50 a month. The leader of this group had the honour to present to this house a petition signed by over a quarter of a million people of all ages urging the government to make that provision. I have here on my desk a whole stack of letters, resolutions and briefs, as have many other hon. members, urging us to take those steps. I believe that many of the members on the government side of the house are in sympathy with w'hat I am saying; all that is required is for the government to decide whether they will take that step on a national basis, or whether they will not.
I also want to say that to me one of the most disappointing things was the fact that no mention was made of removing the means test. Another disappointment was the fact that the provisions for blind persons' pensions remain practically the same as before; particularly is that so as to the age. In my opinion the means test is the most objectionable feature of the present Old Age Pensions Act. Any hon. member who goes through his correspondence on old age pensions will find, I think, that nine out of ten letters he receives stem from the means test provision. People cannot understand the way in which the whole thing operates, to start with; and when they begin to fill in the old age pension 83166-281J
application form, a copy of which I hold in my hand, they find that they are in for a nightmare. It can truly be called a cradle-to-the-grave affair, because on the first page, in question 8, it asks for the date of birth and place of birth; and on the last page, in question 41, it asks, "Who will be in charge of your affairs following your death?" There they have you from birth to death and almost everything in between. I can give a few samples. Question 15 reads:
Give particulars of children living with you or with whom you are living.
They want the name in full, sex, age, occupation, married or single, number of dependent children, income during the past year, contributions. Not only that, but in the next question they say:
Give particulars of children not living with you.
How in the world would you expect anyone to know all about their children who were not living with them, when some might perhaps be living in a foreign country? Again they ask for all the particulars I enumerated under the previous question. Then we go on to page 4 and we find question 32 which reads:
Give date and amount of each contribution to your support by each member of your family during the year prior to making application.
That is another question which is almost impossible to answer. Then question 33:
If any members of your family have failed to contribute give names and reasons for said failure to assist.
It would take a Philadelphia lawyer and a couple of assistants to fill out a form of that kind. How can the old age pensioner know why any of his children or other members of his family failed to assist him? He is required to give reasons why they did not do so. Then there is question 37:
How have you been meeting living expenses during the past year?
That is a ridiculous question. What business is it of anyone how a person has managed to live within the last year? I have already quoted question 41, but it wants to know who is to be in charge of your funeral. I have other forms that go with it, and there are plenty of these. One asks for the assessment of the property owned by the applicant or his or her spouse, in detail. They want to know everything. In fact, under one of the questions, question 30, they' ask you to give the value and description of the furniture, farm equipment or any other property not yet specified. If you happened to have a couple
Old Age Pensions

of pipes and a few pipe cleaners and forgot to put them down, you possibly would be accused of having falsified your application.
The thing becomes ridiculous, and the reason for that is that the application must, of necessity, be based on the regulations which are in force. I am not criticizing the pension authorities who drew up the application form. They had to ask questions to cover all the regulations which are in force under this act. It is because these regulations are ridiculous that the application form is a nightmare, that it is nosey and confusing, and that it is almost impossible for the ordinary person to answer the questions without legal assistance. All that is based on the fact that we have a means test. If there were no means test; if the old age pension were payable to all people as a matter of right-in the same way as family allowances are paid, for example-it would then be unnecessary for every person to go through that nightmare; and it would also be unnecessary to send out, twice a year, a letter or form which has to be filled out-almost as complicated as the other one-to prove that you have not received five cents from anyone else while you were receiving your pension cheque. All that could be wiped out and we should then have our pensions on a commonsense basis. Therefore,	had	the
Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and those associated with him included in this bill a provision to wipe out the means test, I believe that in itself would have been a great step forward in providing a proper system of old age pensions.
I now want to come back to the other disappointment I mentioned, namely, the fact that the age limit for the blind still remains at forty. I have here resolutions and briefs from various organizations making representations on behalf of blind persons, asking that the age limit be lowered. In his speech the other day, the leader of our group advocated that the age limit should be lowered to the point where the family allowance stops; in other words, that at the age of seventeen they should become eligible for the blind pension. That seems 'i be only common sense because, after the age of dependence ends and he or she is not eligible until the age of forty, there is a gap there of almost twenty years, and sometimes more than twenty years, in which the blind person has absolutely nowhere to turn for assistance, except to charity.
While I am at it I also want to say that I had expectedi that the government would sooner or later make some provision to pay the old age pension to Indians, but apparently nothing has been done in that respect. All

I can say is that our record so far, in our treatment of these people, has not been the best and leaves much to be desired. I hope that in the future they will be included.
I was particularly interested in listening the other day to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) speaking on behalf of the Conservative party-and what I want to say now is not said in any spirit of carping criticism- and in listening this afternoon to the hon. member for Eghnton (Mr. Fleming) who was speaking vigorously and with great volume. I was reminded that on a previous occasion he accused me of shedding crocodile tears. I am not going to go that far. I want to be far more charitable to him and his party than he was to me. But as the leader of the opposition spoke, I remembered that I had an advertisement which appeared during the Portage la Prairie by-election; and it struck me as being a little incongruous that the same party which advocated such drastic cutting down of expenditure by this government were now advocating the spending of more money for social security. I want to say clearly that I am not criticizing them in any way for advocating greater expenditures on social security, particularly under this measure, because we are on the same side on this question. But I believe that if the policy advocated during the Portage la Prairie by-election had been followed by this government it would have been impossible, not only to increase the amount of the old age pension, but to pay any old age pension at all, or to pay any family allowances at all. Why do I say that? I have an advertisement here, with the picture of the genial member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller); and incidentally it is a very fine picture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to open my remarks by referring to a word which the previous speaker emphasized, and which he extracted from, speeches made by two hon. members on this side of the house during the debate on this matter a year or two ago. The hon. gentleman objects to the word "premature", as it was used at that time. If I may, to please him I would use that word again today and say that in my opinion this debate is premature. We all agree on the principle involved in this amending bill, which is the improvement of the Old Age Pensions Act; but most of the criticism that has been heard here should have been reserved for the committee of the whole when this bill was considered clause by clause. This is a money bill. No hon. member can do anything to increase its provisions, and a great deal of time is being wasted without any benefit. I had intended to make a few remarks during the committee stage; but since the debate has taken the trend it has taken, I feel that, coming from the province of Quebec, I should voice my opinion.
I do not intend to speak at length; but what I should like to emphasize, first, is that, despite the criticism we have heard yesterday and today on this point, for the past twenty years this party has been interested actively in old age pensions. The first bill was introduced, in 1927; and if one will refer to the various steps which have been taken since then to improve the original statute, he will realize at once that our system of pensions has developed gradually during those twenty years.
The opposition is not satisfied with the milestone we reached today with the amendment contained in this bill. I would repeat what has been said by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), that this measure will bring our system on a par with other systems in force in countries having a similar constitutional complexion. I refer more particularly to New Zealand, Great Britain and the United States.
I would say to hon. members opposite that old age pensions legislation has been on the
	*
statute books of New Zealand for the past fifty years, while in Canada we have had it for only twenty years. Yet, during that half century New Zealand has covered only about the same distance we have covered in less than half the time. The same statement could be made if a comparison were made between our system and that in other countries to wdiich I have referred.
I would emphasize the fact that our government has been more interested in the broader picture of social security. Listening to some opposition members, one would think they are concentrating, all their thought and action upon old age pensions. I believe it would be unwise to act as some of our critics are acting at the present time with respect to this matter, because since the beginning of the last world war more particularly, social security' at large, and as an over-all scheme for the protection of our freedoms and privileges, has been in the minds of the people, not only in this country, but in countries throughout the world.
Our people are not thinking in terms of this or that piece of legislation as much as in terms of a system for which our country fought during the last war, a system of security for each and all of us in our way of life, and to cover our various requirements. This state of mind developed more particularly after the Atlantic charter gave expression to certain principles in August, 1941. To the principles contained in that charter, Canada has subscribed through her acceptance of the declarations of the united nations signed in Washington on January 1, 1942, and we have subscribed on a great number of other occasions in the years following.
As all hon. members know, the principles of freedom proclaimed in the Atlantic charter were the foundation upon which was built the constitution of the united nations organization and they have served as guiding lights to the various committees set up under its supervision and control.
Our country has not delayed unduly her action to implement the obligations she has assumed jointly with the other united nations. On March 8, 1943, this house appointed a select committee whose order of reference was to examine and to report upon a national plan of social insurance which would constitute a charter on social security for the whole of Canada. The committee sat during the session of 1943, was reconstituted in 1944 and did a great amount of work.
In the course of a debate such as this, which deals with old age pensions, it is proper that one should ask himself what importance he should attach to the setting up of an overall scheme of social secuiity, and what place

Old Age Pensions
old age pensions should have in such a scheme. I was particularly interested in the views expressed before the special committee which sat in 1944, by the then executive director of the Canadian welfare council, a gentleman who, since that time, has been honoured with the appointment to the important post of deputy minister of welfare in the dominion government. To precise questions on this point, Doctor Davidson offered the following order of priority:
1.	The maintenance of the fullest possible measure of employment;
2.	The establishment of adequate minimum wage levels;
3.	Children's allowances;
4.	Health insurance;
5.	Old age and retirement insurance.
Before the close of the last war, parliament
agreed to and passed important measures of social security which have done much to bring our country into line with other leading nations of the world. I refer more particularly to the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Family Allowances Act, and an important step was taken with the establishment of a special department for national health and welfare.
How has our government acted in the matter of expressing its firm belief in the necessity for setting up an over-all and comprehensive system of complete social security in Canada? I have already placed on record the expert views of a gentleman who certainly had sufficient knowledge and experience to express such views.
The minister referred to the fact that the national health programme represented a great gap in our social security programme, and he pointed out the necessity of improving our old age pensions.
The federal authorities have held, and rightly so, that the only constitutional way to act was to confer with the provinces, and they have done that on several occasions since 1945. They made proposals which involved the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars by this government, provided that those proposals were agreed to by the provinces. More particularly, the scheme of old age pensions which they suggested called for an expenditure of S200 million by this government, while the scheme of health insurance called for an expenditure of $150 million. Family allowances, which have since been put into effect, called for a net expenditure of $200 million by this government.
I do not intend to go over the explanations given by the minister of the amendments provided by this bill. He has stated that this is the maximum pension possible, and he has
stated that there is to be a relaxation of certain restrictions in the application of the means test and so forth. I may have something else to say when the bill is in committee.
At this time I wish to state my views in connection with certain criticisms which we have heard since this discussion commenced. As the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) has said, the foundation of the criticism from all quarters of the opposition seems to be that this measure has been too long delayed and that it provides for only a partial measure of justice to the aged. That is the usual refrain of the opposition, and if one takes the trouble to read Hansard since this parliament opened in 1945 he will notice that in each case the criticism of the opposition has been along the same theme-too little, too late.
I shall not go over the legislative activities of this parliament prior to the last war, but I would point out that Canada has been marching forward and has achieved a success which has placed her in a leading role among the medium nations of the world, in spite of the criticism which we have heard throughout the war and since, that she was doing too little and it was coming too late.
Listening to what has been said on the other side, I wonder what would have been the reaction if the minister had brought in a bill containing the exact proposals of the green book, proposals which have been agreed to by seven out of the nine provinces and which are still waiting for the agreement of the other two. I can hear the criticism by the opposition. I am sure they would have blamed the government for taking an autocratic attitude and for disregarding the rights of the provinces in doing something which had not been agreed to. I do not see any soundness in the stand taken by the opposition on this bill.
We could have waited even longer. The proposals made are definite and concrete. Thej'- were made two years ago and the provinces were invited to cooperate in their realization. There are still two important provinces which have not yet come forward. We could have waited and I think we would have had valid reasons for waiting. However, the government has felt that the aged people should not be penalized by having to wait until the agreement had the signature of all nine provinces. We have today a compromise, a measure which comes halfway between the present system and that contained in the proposals which we had hoped would be accepted by the provinces and by which we would
Old Age Pensions

have had a more comprehensive and complete social security programme in Canada.
Criticism has been heard with reference to the means test, but there has been no mention of the fact that the countries which have been compared with Canada., such as New Zealand, Great Britain and the United States, still have the means test. They are in the process of transition toward an over-all contributory plan. After twenty years of operating our old age pensions in Canada, it is our hope-and I believe that is shared by hon. members in every corner of the house-that some day, with the cooperation of the provinces, we shall have a contributory old age pension plan in Canada.
It has been suggested during the debate that if this bill provided for hospitalization, medical, dental and optical care for our aged people, it would be much more acceptable. But this suggestion does not strike me as being quite in order, since all these matters are under provincial jurisdiction, and I do not see what more we can do until all the provinces agree to allow us to enter these fields. These hon. members have certainly not followed the reaction in some of the provinces when we were discussing health insurance in the committee of this house on social security three or four years ago.
Suggestions have been made to increase the maximum pension payable to S50 at the age of sixty. Others are advocating the payment of a pension of $60 at the age of sixty, but I do not see any soundness in these proposals. I cannot see any argument to support them, unless at the same time it is advocated that our taxation should be set up at a higher level in order to meet these additional expenditures. From the estimate of our population for next year, a pension of $50 at age sixty would cost $850 million. This is nearly as much as the estimated receipts from the income and corporation taxes for the fiscal year 1946-47. If the pension were put at $60 at the age of sixty the cost would exceed the receipts from these two taxes and would involve an expenditure of over one billion dollars.
I should like to have heard something about the fiscal system which would be advocated to meet the requirements of all these proposals that we hear about for additional benefits or services or to increase those that we already have, such as old age pensions. If hon. members on the other side are sincere when they say that we should aim at a coordinated social security programme which would provide for every hazard that a man is apt to come up against in modern society, they might give more importance to coopera-

tion between the provinces and to the necessity of an agreement between those to whom our constitution has particularly entrusted the responsibility to take care of these hazards and needs of our population. I do not see that anything worth while can be achieved in the field of social security when considering an over-all long-range scheme, unless we discuss at the same time our constitution and the cooperation that we need. To lay down any durable foundation for the future of our country, as is done in the proposals to the provinces with regard to old age pensions, we should not just pick out that particular hazard by itself and offer to spend $600 million or $700 million or more every year and give old age pensions to a greater number of our citizens. We have aimed, first, to cover a wider field; we have given a place of importance to old age pensions, and we have given a more important place to a service which our country does not have, to help ensure a national health programme with the intent of filling the important gap and with tha desire of laying the basis for a continual and worth-while alleviation of the difficulties and needs of our population. I think we have a balanced programme of social legislation already in our statutes and in the proposals to the provinces. It is the duty of hon. members, as it is the duty of the citizens of Canada, to impress upon the provinces which have not as yet agreed to these proposals, the necessity of concurring with their sister provinces in helping to lay down a foundation for a social future for our country.
Coming from Quebec, I could not conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, without pointing to what the situation is in my province. The province of Quebec entered into agreements with the federal authorities with regard to oldi age pensions in 1936. In the years following, until the war broke out, nothing was done by Quebec to increase the maximum pension payable to our destitute and needy citizens. It is true that during the war, from 1939 to 1945. a good excuse could be offered for not doing so; but for the past two years, if one bears in mind that the provincial budget has had substantial surpluses, if one has regard for the economic and financial position of Quebec as compared with that of the other provinces, one cannot avoid asking himself how it is that in Quebec there is but $25 as maximum pension payable to the aged. The example set up by our neighbour province of Ontario today should be an invitation to Quebec and to its neighbour provinces to get closer to the other provinces and to the federal government in a true association and partnership in the working out

Old Age Pensions
of a greater future for our country. The first step that Quebec could take toward that aim would be to take the necessary steps for the immediate voting of increased pensions. I would not be satisfied until such time as Quebec is on the same level as the great provinces of British Columbia and Ontario as far as the alleviation of the lot of all our old people is concerned.
May I refer to a statement which was made on the 16th instant by the provincial treasurer of Quebec, Hon. Onesime Gagnon, at the bankers' convention in the state of New York. The statement is in the French language, but I may say, from what the newspaper La Presse reported in its issue of the 17th instant, that if the Quebec provincial treasurer would translate into legislative action the feelings to which he gave expression on the occasion of that convention, Quebec would no longer consider Ottawa as a foreign country; Quebec would no longer consider her sister provinces as competitors from whom she should keep away in case they might lean against her and infringe upon her privileges, traditions and rights. I would hope that Mr. Gagnon would communicate to his leader the premier of Quebec the spirit which he has there expressed and that from now on there will be between Quebec and Ottawa the same spirit of partnership as Mr. Gagnon preached between Canada and the United States in the course of his statement. This is what he said. I quote in the French language:
(Translation):
Only the close cooperation between the United States and Canada, can prevent the catastrophe of a third world war, which would surely destroy civilization.
(Text) :
And later on, Mr. Speaker, he said:
(Translation):
The Canadians and the Americans, united in their love of freedom, struggle for the progress of civilization. Both countries are staunch supporters of the federal system and both are equally interested in the return of peace to the universe. To achieve these aims they must cooperate and such cooperation is bound to ensure important results.
Mr. Gagnon said to the 600 delegates assembled here since Saturday. "That there can be no question of staying aloof or of minding our local business alone."

It woidd appear, Mr. Speaker, that for the past two years, if the Hon. Mr. Gagnon is sincere in his statement, there has been some progress in the attitude of the provincial government of Quebec toward 83166-282
the government of any place outside the province. I hope that what I have read will be true so far as the relations between the provincial government and the federal government are concerned. I trust that we may expect closer cooperation between the two governments, to start with, in order to improve the situation of the aged of the province of Quebec, and, in the second place, in order to build for Canada a great future, social security in the province of Quebec, in the whole of Canada, which would be better, and in the whole world-and that is what Mr. Gagnon had in mind the other day. That is, I am sure, the aim of each person of good will on this continent and elsewhere.
Mr. PATRICK H. ASHBY (Edmonton East): The old age pensions bill we have before us should never have been drawn up in the first place, and, in the second place, it should never have been brought before this house, because it is none of our business.- Here are we assembled like a lot of old bachelors discussing among ourselves, as it were, whether or not Mrs. Murphy's kids should have peanuts or popcorn. Let me illustrate what I mean when I say it is none of our business.
When I was a little boy "my mammy done told me" that God was a great and good being, that He was all that was right, just and honourable, but that there was another called the devil, who was the very opposite, and I often wondered as a child why God permitted the devil to hang around. Over a quarter of a century ago I dissociated myself from artificial entities and dealt only in realities. In other words, I went back to the farm where I became intimately acquainted with nature, with God if you like, and, having in mind since childhood the puzzling fact of the devil and God existing side by side, I asked God one day, figuratively speaking, of course, why He did not knock the devil out of Old Nick and be done with it. The answer I got made me stagger back on my heels. My mouth opened, my eyes nearly bursting from my head, for the answer I got was: Demon est deus inversus. "You", I said in amazement, "don't say so". Well, isn't that queer, that it never occurred to us before? I began to see and to realize things that I had never seen or understood before, and one was that we merely have things turned wrong side out, upside down. That is all that is the matter. Put things right side up and everything is all right. There is nothing to it.
Getting bolder, still figuratively speaking, I asked God if He minded my taking His place for a while. "Oh," I hastened to explain, "I do not mean I want to dominate the world. I am not an internationalist, a communist. I

Old Age Pensions

do not even want to dominate Canada. I am not a bureaucrat, a socialist. I do not even want to dominate our old folks; I do not even want to set their standard of living. All I want to be is a small god', a little bitty god on my own farm, over some pigs and sheep." "Sure", He said, "go ahead". So I clambered onto a pedestal, which happened to be a mound thrown out of the barn door, driving off the barnyard rooster, who had been flapping his wings and crowing to the world like a politician at election time. Climbing to the top of it, I raised my hand and said, "Let there be life" and there was life; for, as I said before, I was dealing in realities and not in artificial entities. I was not dealing with pens and pencils, with paper and figures, with words, with budgets and estimates and old age pensions. I was dealing with chromosomes, and determiners, germ cells, with living things. I was dealing with life itself, and, having created life of my own choosing, I discovered many interesting and instructive things, among which was that I must not interfere with the freedom of any individual under my care. I also learned that there was one Divine right that I must never encroach upon, and that Divine right is this: We have no right to take from one to give to another. I am making this statement, that any human being who takes part in this taxation swindle is committing a crime, not merely against his fellow man, but against the Almighty God, who has that Divine right, and Him alone.

speechtext:
Taxation, yes. We have no right to tax anybody. There was a time when human beings believed that a king had that divine right, but at the time of magna carta we took that divine right away from kings and introduced checks and balances which governed taxation. Today this divine right is being usurped by bureaucrats who claim they can force their fellow human beings to hand over to them money which belongs by right to those who earn it. Taxation results in all this confusion. Taxation is robbery. Taxation alienates production, or goods, from the people who are the rightful owners.
I should just like to point out one or two things, Mr. Speaker. So much has already been said, and I do not want to repeat too much, but here is a typical case, a little old lady who writes as follows:
I am a widow, sixty years of age. What is there in life for us? Many people think there is a widows' pension; they are confused with the mothers' allowance which does not help a widow of this age.
We are old, tired, and afraid of the future . . .
All the discussion on lowering the age limit for the old age pension is good but in the meantime many widows are desperate and afraid.
[Mr. Ashby.)
Then -we talk about freedom from fear! What a sham I Here are poor old souls who live in fear. They know not where the next meal is coming from. I have a soft spot in my heart for the ladies, and when I was in the city of Edmonton I spotted a dandy across on the other side of the street. She was just like a little partridge hurrying through a crowded barnyard, ready to take off at any moment. There being no policeman around, I took after her, breaking the traffic rules. I caught up to her after a while, puffing and blowing like a grampus. I raised my hat to her and told her who I was. I am a kind of mind-reader, and she said to herself, "So what?" and grabbed her handbag all the tighter. I took her by the sleeve of her coat. No wonder she was backing away from me because she had a hammer handle in it; that is, I thought it was a hammer handle until I saw her hand dangling on the end of it. She had no meat on her bones at all. I do not think that poor little soul would have weighed over seventy pounds. I think I could have picked her up like a suitcase and carried her home. And what hands she had, tool-lined with dirt, broken fingernails. Her clothes were old but neatly mended. I got into conversation with her, and this is the little story she told me. She was over seventy. She earned her living at odd jobs-picking berries, digging potatoes, weeding people's gardens, doing charwoman's work, doing any job at all. But her eyes showed nothing but fear. There was no smile of happiness on her face. That was right here in Canada, in the city of Edmonton, Alberta, in this day and age. Can you imagine it?

What is the solution? I am not going to take up very much more time, Mr. Speaker, because so much else has been said. The solution is to free every individual. Who are we to decide whether others shall have their freedom or not? Once they get their freedom, suitable education will enable all these old folks to enjoy their remaining years in their own way. I think that is all I need to say.
To sum up, I might once more say that we must get rid of this bureaucratic rule or statism. We have an abundance of experts. If they do not know how to do the jobs, it is time we discharged them from office. We know what our old folks want. If we put it up to a vote throughout Canada I am sure they would soon let us know. speechtext:
I am rather nervous in rising tonight, Mr. Speaker, following a member from Alberta. I cannot exactly understand why anybody in Alberta should be entirely short of money. I understood that everybody in that province received at least $25 a month. Inasmuch as I have had something to say in the past about quoting from notes, and since I intend to quote quite extensively, in order that there may be no misunderstanding I would suggest that a member of the Conservative party and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) sit on either side of me to see that I am not reading my speech when, in fact, I am quoting.
Strange to say, though I support this government, I do not at all like the bill that has been introduced. I do not think it goes far enough; I do not believe the people in my riding think it goes far enough. Early in 1943 we from 83166-282J
British Columbia sitting on this side of the house were not satisfied with the Old Age Pensions Act of that day and appointed a member from our province to represent us. The member we appointed is now in the other place, to which I am not permitted to refer as I should very much like to. He was a distinr-guished member of this house, the former member from Burrard and mayor of the third largest city in Canada, which in a few years will be the largest city. These recommendations were unanimous, though two of our members at that time were serving overseas. I endorsed the recommendations on behalf of the hon>. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), as his representative here. He was a squadron leader in the R.C.A.F., serving in Africa at that time. I simply give this explanation to show that our recommendations, which were made to the leader of our party in British Columbia and to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), were unanimous on the part of the British Columbia members on this side of the house. I want to quote what we recommended at that time:
1.	An amendment to the constitution making old age pensions a federal responsibility.
2.	Reduction of the age limit. In the case of men from seventy to sixty-five years and in the case of women from seventy to sixty years.
3.	Increase in the maximum amount payable from $20 per month to $1 a day.
4.	Removal of the onerous and restrictive regulation now in force.
5.	In addition to the existing old age pension system the establishment of a contributory system as a part of our unemployment insurance scheme now in operation.
6.	Similar adjustments for the blind veterans in need and invalids.
To follow that up, I should like to quote also what the special committee on social security, set up by this parliament, recommended in its report on July 23, 1943:
That the government review the existing regulations governing old age pensions, pensions for the blind and war veterans' allowances, and consider the advisability of adjusting the eligibility age to a lower level, and of increasing the amount of pensions. That an investigation be made into conditions and bases of grants of these pensions in the various provinces, cost of subsistence, inequalities, responsibility for and distribution of obligation, and all the matters relating to the problems involved, in order to effect greater coordination, equality and adequate adjustments.
At that time I was speaking, as I think I am still speaking, for the British Columbia members. If our recommendations had received the full support of all the provinces in 1943 the present inadequate bill would not have been brought down now. This matter was discussed in the house on April 1 and July 4, 1943. At that time the present Min-
Old Age Pensions

ister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was Minister of Finance. I have the greatest admiration for him, because I know he has the greatest ability of any man in Canada to say no. On July 24, 1943, he announced an increase in old age pensions from S20 to $25 a month; that is at page 5490 of Hansard for that year. My point is that if in 1943 it required $25 a month, for the Minister who is sponsoring this bill to tell me this increase from $25 to $30 a month meets the present cost of living just does not add up. In July, 1943, the then premier of Ontario agreed to carry on the increase of S3 a month in this province, and British Columbia agreed to $5 a month. At that time the British Columbia members on this side of the house pointed out to the provincial premiers that we thought the age should be lowered. We did not go only to our own premier; we went further and tried to convince even Ontario that this should be done. In fact we wrote the premiers of all the provinces. We thought we had a very good reason for doing this. We believed in a contributory old age pension scheme; but, pending that, we felt the old age pensions should be adequate, because it was obvious that people now in receipt of these pensions were not in a position and should not be asked to contribute.
I now want to quote from a man who, I think, has done more for old age pensions in Canada than any other man in this country; a man who, I believe, has at heart the interests of the old age pensioners as much as any man in Canada, if not more. I refer to the present Prime Minister, my leader. I think this ought to be good enough. I am referring to pages 2260 and 2261 of Hansard for June 2. 1931; and when I am through, I am sure the minister sponsoring this bill will bring in an amendment to bring it into line with what I think it should be. This is what the Prime Minister said:
The Liberal administration fought for many years for an old age pension act. and care I think was taken to make it clear that an amendment to the British North America Act would be required before this federal government would have power to administer an old age pension scheme. It was recognized that an amendment to the British North America Act would take some time, and for that reason the government of the day adopted the method of agreeing to give these grants in aid to the provinces on condition that they would carry out a scheme framed by the federal government which would be similar in all the provinces.
An hon. Member : A vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The principle, from a
financial point of view, was unsound. I am quite prepared to concede that. But I will go a step further and say that, in my opinion, this parliament ought to remedy the unsoundness of the principle, not by discontinuing to vote money for

old age pensions, but by assuming the entire obligation, one hundred per cent. This government should take over the whole scheme and itself pay out the money. That is the position that should be taken; that is the proper way to remedy what there is of unsoundness in the principle . . .
Obviously the principle is thoroughly sound. I have always taken that position and have fought strenuously for it; and to get that principle recognized by parliament I was prepared to go so far as to support a grant in aid, which I am perfectly frank to admit was, from the point of view of financing, an unsound method. Now I say, let us recognize that the principle of old age pensions itself is perfectly sound and involves an obligation which the federal parliament should assume. Let us undertake to administer the Old Age Pensions Act from Ottawa and have all the moneys which are necessary for the payment of those pensions voted by this parliament.
I believe that policy has been reaffirmed by the Prime Minister on other occasions. We from British Columbia on this side of the house, after hearing the then minister of finance on April 1, 1943, wrote our provincial premier, with copies to the premiers of all the provinces, giving our understanding of the policy then laid down:
il. The responsibility for old age pensions is primarily of provincial jurisdiction;
2.	The amount paid to old age pensioners is inadequate;
3.	The dominion government will not contribute any portion of any increase in the amount payable;
4.	The provincial governments are now in a better position to meet the cost of old age pensions than is the dominion government;
5.	The dominion government will give consideration to a request made by substantially all of the provinces for a reconsideration of the maximum limit in the Old Age Pensions Act (as outlined on pages 1789 to 1793 of Hansard April 1, 1943.)
That was our conception of the policy of the then minister of finance. We were not in accord with that. We wrote to our provincial premier and to the premiers of the provinces as follows:
That the British North America Act be amended to nationalize old age pensions;
That the age limit be reduced;
That the maximum payable be raised;
That many of the arbitrary restrictions now in the act, and the regulations, be repealed; .
That the policy adopted for old age pensioners should be extended to include pensions to the blind, and mothers' allowances.
And note this, that this is the recommendation by members from British Columbia in the House of Commons, recommendations to our premier in 1943. We continued:
That the proportion paid by the federal government for pensions and administration should, pending the amendment to the constitution, be increased to 99 per cent.

Old Age Pensions
The reason we thought that, and still think it, is that we realize it takes time to amend the constitution. Some may think it takes too much time, but the fact is it takes time to amend it. However, while it takes time to amend the British North America Act, it takes no time to make a grant in aid to a province. That could be done tomorrow by this parliament.
I should like to quote just a few figures; because, frankly, I do not like the present bill. I do not think it meets conditions as they exist today. I for one cannot understand why in a country with our vast resources we do not give more thought to our greatest resource, the youth of our country. We financed' the war through taxation and borrowing; and we financed our borrowing on the strength of our resources. Let us recognize that our greatest resource is the youth of our country. This country was built up by our pioneers, and we owe them a pension which would be adequate- not charity, but a pension which is due to the pioneers of this country.

In this connection I wish to quote the words of my leader, a man who, in my opinion, has done more for the unfortunate people in this country than anyone else has done. I speak as an old-time Liberal, one of the few free traders on this side of the house-

The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I quote the Prime Minister as of March 26, 1926, as he is reported at page 1976 of Hansard:
If we were legislating as my hon. friend has suggested, for young people of the age of ten or twelve; if we were providing an old age scheme for page boys about the house, for schoolboys and girls, then it would be wise to lay emphasis upon the importance of a contribution on their part towards a system intended to help to maintain them in their old age. But I take it that this house at the present time, in discussing old age pensions, is not thinking of your people of ten, twenty or thirty years of age or even of persons of forty or fifty years of age. We are thinking more particularly of that large body of men and women now in Canada who are approaching the age of seventy years. We have in mind those between the ages of sixty and seventy who are finding it difficult to get the assurance that their declining years are not going to be spent in dependence on charity.
In the course of the debate today reference has been made to the old age pension scheme as though it were something related particularly to inmates of poorhouses. I am inclined to feel that there is no class in human society today that has not in its numbers a very considerable percentage of persons who are living in- constant dread of the moment when, in their advanced years, they will be thrown upon their children or upon society for support.
One of the greatest needs in the industrial life of Canada today is that the standards governing industrial relations should be more or less identical as between one province and another. That can only be brought about by some kind of action on the part of the federal government leading to cooperation between the federal government and the provinces and among the different provinces themselves. I submit that this scheme of old age pensions as here drafted will have that effect.
It will be the natural thing to ask the representatives of the provincial governments to meet with the departments of the federal government which may be administering the old age pensions plan, to discuss further its details, and to consider the regulations for its effective operation.
I do not see why old age pensioners throughout Canada should be penalized because of the selfishness of two provinces which claim to have the greatest population and the greatest wealth, which has been built up at the expense of the test of Canada. I refer to

Insofar as it may be practicable, having regard to Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence, old age and other disability should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces. It took time to gain that end. It was a new field for a federal administration to enter. Old age pensions appeared to be the obvious place to begin. It was possible to obtain the cooperation of the provinces for such a measure more readily than for one respecting unemployment, invalidity or health insurance. An old age pensions measure was enacted by the Liberal administration in office in 1927.

You have your choice and there can be no buts or ifs about it. We are not living in the ox-cart days, at least in British Columbia; we are living in the modern, atomic age. I want to tell the minister that I am a supporter of this government and I intend to support this bill, just as do my hon. friends opposite, because half a loaf is better than nothing. Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of being on the first committee appointed to consider old age pensions. From the evidence giveni before us at that time. I came to the conclusion that a pension of $50 a month should be paid to the people of Canada who had reached the age of sixty or sixty-five years and that this should be a federal responsibility. I was alone in the committee in that regard, but I have not seen any good reason to change my mind on the matter up to this time.
I should like to preface my remarks with a brief quotation from an official summary of the legislation of the state of Washington providing for old age pensions. This states:
On no other issue are the people of the state of Washington as well as our nation as united as they are in the recognition of the economic and social necessity of returning to our senior citizens, the fathers and mothers of our country, part of the wealth which their labour helped to create.
I imagine that is the sentiment of this house. There is no issue upon which there is so much unanimity in Canada as that of the need of taking care of our older people. As a matter of fact old age pensions are not of interest only to our older people; they are of equal interest to our young people. Many
times it relieves them of burdens which they are unable to bear, the burden of taking care of old parents, or grandfathers and grandmothers. But apart from that, if any person in Canada is lucky enough to live long enough he may want an old age pension. So it matters not how you consider the thing, this is an issue which directly affects every one in this dominion.
Most speakers have repeated the statement made by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) to the effect that no party can claim a monopoly of interest in this question. Most certainly I do not make any special claim and I do not think any one has made that claim. We all recognize that it is not a political question in the narrow sense of partisan politics, but we also recognize that it is fundamentally a political as well as an economic question in the wider application of those terms. Nevertheless, while it is not necessarily a partisan political question, there can be no doubt that the views which form the background of party policy do necessarily affect the actions of a party in power with respect to this or any other issue.
I think it is true to say that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who is piloting this bill through the house, did strike a political note in introducing the legislation; and perhaps he merited the criticism which a number of hon. members made to him for having done so. I think, however, that he perhaps made a mistake in his own interests He quoted to us the programme which the Liberal party offered to the people of Canada at the last election. It was a fairly good programme with respect to old age pensions, even though it did not go far enough; but it did propose to increase the amount paid to old age pensioners; it did propose to lower the age at which pensions were to be paid, and it did propose to remove the means test. Of course that is not being done. It is true that they are raising the dominion contribution slightly, so that it makes possible a pension of $50 a month; but I venture to say that if an account should be taken of the increased cost of living as between 1947 and 1926 when the Old Age Pensions Act was originally introduced, the present proposal will grant a pension very much lower in purchasing power to the people of this country than was done in 1926. Therefore this does not really represent an improvement over the original act.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare went on to say that the reason why the programme as promised by his party was not being implemented to the full in this legislation was that the provinces had failed to come

Old Age Pensions
to a satisfactory arrangement with respect to taxation and other matters of interprovincial and dominion importance. In this way he found for himself an excuse, if not a reason, for the limited advance which he is proposing in his legislation. Then he rose in his place today when some hon. member from the Progressive Conservative party was speaking and suggested that the legislation now proposed had so stimulated the premier of Ontario that he had come forward with a proposal to pay $40 a month old age pensions to the people of that province. I thought that was very well counteracted by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) when he pointed out that, in doing so, the premier of Ontario was doing what this legislation or the parliament of Canada had failed to do for all the provinces of this dominion. But I think the argument might be carried beyond that. It is time that Premier Drew has been one of the stubborn figures that have prevented a satisfactory arrangement between the provinces and the dominion-

I am- not blaming, him; he may have had a good idea. I am only pointing out the fact, and he might now very well say to the other provinces which have accepted the agreement: "Look, our province which did not accept the agreement is now paying $40 a month and you have to be satisfied with $30 or less as the case may be." Therefore I think from a political point of view' the minister -was perhaps not as astute in the particular efforts that- he made as he usually is.
In this connection I should like to say that I deplore the inequity which is likely to develop between the provinces in a matter of this kind, an inequity which is inexcusable and indefensible. The fact that British Columbia may have a little greater natural wealth than some of the other provinces and may be able to pay a little more to its older people is no reason why people in another province with a little less natural resources from which to draw should have to receive less; especially let us say, people living in the city of Winnipeg, living in a country which is very cold in the winter time, where older people need more warm clothes, more coal to keep them warm, a better house in which to live and such improvements as must be available in a country with a climatic condition as

speechtext:
All right, at any time, and where they can live on less food of certain kinds. It seems ridiculous that there should be that disparity. I am emphasizing this point, sir, that whatever amount of pension is paid in Canada must be paid on the basis of Canadian citizenship; that to be done in that way it must be fundamentally a federal responsibility, and to allow this hole-in-the-corner business to go on is representing a viewpoint that is beyond comment.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), in commenting on the bill, had something to say about the necessity of changing the constitution. I have no doubt that it may be wise and necessary to change the constitution here and there. But I want to point out to him and to the house that the same constitutional right which the government now exercises in paying a pension of $30 a month at the age of seventy with a means test can enable them to pay S50 a month at sixty-five without a means test. There is no fundamental change in the constitution which will differentiate between a pension of $30 a month and a pension of $50.
Most of the speakers from all sides of the house have indicated in this debate that they intend to vote for the measure. I will not go so far as that at this moment; I am not so sure about it. The other day I was reading a letter from an old pensioner who said virtually this: "I cannot live on $30 a month. I am less than existing, and if it is not going to be improved sufficiently to make an existence possible it might be better to stop it altogether and end the matter much more quickly." That is the view of a pensioner. Perhaps the house would not wish to go that far with him, but still there is a good deal of logic and reason in what he says. Everybody admits that $30 a month is too little for one to live on. Well, if they cannot live on $30, what do they live on when they have nothing to live on but $30? They try to eke out an existence which gradually saps their strength until they tumble into the grave a few years sooner than they otherwise would. That is a miserable way for our old people to end their lives. Moreover, taking the argument that if we vote against this measure it may appear to the old age pensioners that we are depriving them of the proposed increase

Old Age Pensiom
of $5 a month, by that same logic we would be prevented from amending this bill at any time in a manner that is worth while, and sooner or later we shall have to do what I once heard a French-Canadian friend of mine, who got a little mixed up in his English idioms, say: "Some time we will have to grab that bull by the tail and look her straight in the eye." I say that some day we shall have to face up to this issue and not be afraid of its political implications. The fact that we stand for a greater pension may for the moment put us in the position of being opposed to the pension bill which is now before us.
The burden of criticism so far levelled at the bill by those who are opposing it may be summarized, and I shall summarize it, very briefly; because the same road must be travelled by me in this regard as by others. I do not wish to weary the house by going into details and an elaborate comment on joints that have already been dealt with pretty thoroughly by a number of speakers. But perhaps I may put it in a little different language and do so briefly.
The first and most obvious, criticism is that the pension is too little. It may be assumed that a little of something is better than nothing of anything. I think that much may be said for the bill: A little of something is better than nothing of anything. But $30 a month is not enough for anyone to live on in Canada. The minister himself admits that. He said it was not enough.

I am going by the bill, and if the minister can show me how it produces more than that, and how it might not produce less, I shall be glad to listen to him when he replies to some of the questions that have been asked by a number of speakers, who have taken the same view of the legislation that I am now taking. As I say, if we have misinterpreted the bill, then, in the first place, the minister has no one to blame for that but himself. He should have spent his time in telling us exactly what the legislation does mean instead of leaving us to interpret it for ourselves and then saying that we have not the right, interpretation of it. Instead of that, he spent much of his time in building up party propaganda, which, I think, may be a boomerang and come back at him later.
It has been mentioned in the debate that not only is the $30 a month too little for any individual; but in the case where the old age pensioner, the head of the house, has a wife, who is younger than he is by a few years, he still has to maintain his wife. This view was
first expressed in this house, so far as I am aware, by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), and I believe it has been implemented in the soldiers pension act. But the point I want to emphasize is not only that, in the case of a man who has reached the age of seventy, who has a wife of sixty-five, that thirty dollars has to do both of them. I would point out the case of the woman whose husband has died before she gets any pension at all. I had a letter yesterday from an elderly lady about sixty-five years of age, whose husband had just died of cancer, and she told me that, in order to pay the hospital bill and bury her husband, she had sold their cows and even their chickens. There are no pensions for widows of that type in any of our provinces. She is left absolutely stranded. She is not able to work for a living, and she has no means, until she reaches the age of seventy, of receiving any income at all. How she is to reach the age of seventy without any income at all is more than I am able to say.
The minister frankly admits that $30 is not enough. But if it is not enough, why is it not enough? I reiterate the question put by the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):	On what basis were the calculations made? How did the government arrive at $30? What was the object of arriving at $30 if it were not to make it possible for the older people to live on that amount? I want to emphasize again that if the people of Canada, with our great wealth of natural resources, with the extent to which modern science has been applied to production, with our great plant equipment and our capital equipment, and with our technical skills, can produce the food and clothing as well as the homes necessary to keep our old people in decency during the last years of their lives, then there is no reason under heaven for stopping them from getting what is necessary.
Can that be done ? Can we produce enough for our older people, or must we submit to a condition under which the old people of Canada must be allowed to go on suffering under an inadequate provision during their old age? I say, in the first place, that we can produce more than ample of the goods required for sustaining the lives, not only of our aged' people, but of all our people.- The Minister of Finance, (Mr. Abbott) indicated that our production in Canada this year will reach $12,000,000,000. That is a considerable income for the nation and represents a vast advance over 1926, when this legislation was originally passed. But I suggest to the minister that not only can we produce $12,000,000,000 worth, but with the increased facilities of production which the war stim-
Old Age Pensions

ulated we can produce in the next few years very much more goods with even less labour than we did before.
I saw an estimate by a competent statistician in the United States that in 1947 they will be able to produce, with approximately 30,000,000 men, what it required 40,000,000 men to produce in 1938, and I imagine a similar advance has taken place in Canada. So that there are two grounds, as I see it, upon which we should arrive at a pension that should be paid to our older people. The first is, what are the essential needs of our old people, in food1, clothing, shelter and a little bit of the comforts of life? What are the irreducible minimums of services that they require? The second is that our old age pension should either be based on that or be commensurate with the national income when production is in full swing. Those are the underlying principles.
The next point of criticism is that not only is the pension too little, but it is too late. It is too late because many of our older people from sixty to sixty-five and up to seventy die in poverty and misery before they are seventy years of age and never get any pension at all. It would appear to me that the principle behind the present bill is, "Not to many and not for long"; for if we maintain the age limit of seventy it will not be to many; and it will not be for long that those who get it will continue to do so.
I now wish to mention what is done with regard to the age limit and the means test in a few other countries of the world. Denmark pays pensions at sixty and Sweden at sixty-five; Britain, at sixty-five for men and sixty for women; Australia at sixty-five for men and sixty for women; Russia, at sixty for men and fifty-five for women. None of these has a means test at all. With regard to the means test, I think the thrift argument was pretty well exploited. As a matter of fact, it is a double-barreled argument, but I think the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) and my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) fired the same barrel. They pointed out that there was no incentive given to those people who tried to put away a few dollars each year in order' to secure for themselves an annuity at a certain age, because when that time came they were not recompensed as were other citizens who qualified for the old age pension; thus they had little encouragement to save. But. the same argument applies to the old age pensioner himself. Up until this bill came in, I think it was something like $125 a year
which he was allowed to earn, if he could. Here and there there are individuals who might have done a little better than that; but if they did, it was taken away from them or their pension was reduced accordingly. In this bill the amount has been silghtly raised. The limit of the means test has been modified somewhat. But still, if the pensioners received the highest amount they could receive, they still would not have a sufficient income on which to live comfortably in Canada at the present time. The pensioner himself should be allowed to make all that he can, if he can make anything, and his pension should be paid regardless of his income.
The next point is that no permanent plan for adequate old age pension is contemplated in this legislation. I want to emphasize the point of view that my group has constantly put forward, that there should be an over-all social securits^ programme for Canada, which would have to be carried out through federal legislation, whether by cooperation with the provinces or whether by an amendment to the constitution which gives the federal government the complete right to pass such legislation. I do not think we are going to worry about what the actual details of the technique of bringing it into fulfilment may be. What we are interested in is to see that it is brought about. I believe that it can be brought about even under the constitution as it is. But if not, let us take steps to change it.
In the second place, I believe that such a system might very well be contributory. If we look at the amounts which reasonable pensions would involve, we shall see that perhaps it would be wise to have a contributory system started as soon as possible. The programme which the government promised, but which it is not giving, would have cost Canada in 1947 over $550,800,000; in 1951, $731,520,000; and in 1971, $1,100,880,000. I am not worried any more than anybody else about the millions and the billions. Under the system under which we are living, every government must find the means by which this is to be done. That means collecting through taxation under our present system That could very well become a burden in taxation which was too great. But in the last analysis, all our old age pensions must come, somehow, in some way, from the people. It is merely a matter of arrangement. I think it might be advisable for the government to undertake, as quickly as possible, a scheme by which contributions may be made by individuals, starting young, so that very soon we should have a contributory system fully developed which would afford to all

Old Age Pensions
the people of Canada a worth-while income. I am in thorough agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver North. I want to take this opportunity to pay a compliment to that hon. gentleman. I want to congratulate him. He is a brilliant young man and he has shown courage. He stood up for the thing he wanted. In doing that, not only did he do honour to himself, but he honoured the membership of this house; more than that, he honoured the party to which he belongs; for no party which holds within its ranks people who are free to say things, as he was today, can be said to be utterly dead.

I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) on his contribution to this debate. I think he said many things to which the government and the minister might well listen, coming as they do from a member of the government party. I was particularly interested when the hon. member quoted the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1931, in which he said he would go as far as grants in aid to the provinces in order that the dominion might take over the whole cost of old age pensions. I could not help thinking, when I heard those words read, how very far below that principle the Prime Minister and the government have now dropped, and what a great recession from the green book proposals is being made in the measure presented to the house by the minister.
In what was said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, there was only one thing with which I did not agree. He suggested that there was some need to wait, in connection with this matter of old age pensions, until there was a general agreement with the provinces and a new conference. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is no need to wait for a new conference or for fiscal agreement before the policy to which the Prime Minister pledged himself in 1931 is carried out. If the dominion is to take over the full cost of old age pensions for those over seventy years of age, why is there any need to wait? I have here the green book proposals of August, 1945. After referring to the national health programme and pointing out that it provides for dominion assistance to a series of provincially administered health schemes, those proposals go on to say, at page 42:
The proposed system of old age pensions payable as of right without means test to persons seventy or over would be instituted and administered by the dominion government and specific agreements with provincial governments would not be essential to its implementation.
I simply want to say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley and to the minister that there is no justification whatever for the government to hide behind the projected dominion-provincial conference and neglect to implement its green book proposals on old age pensions. I suggest to the hon. member that, instead of getting up as he does and criticizing the government from that side of the house, we shall never have action of the kind he wants as long as he continues to support this government. I want to make this prophecy now, that
Old Age Pensions

the social security programme set out in the green book proposals of 1945 will never be implemented by this government. It is my belief that they have gone a long way from those proposals and that they have no intention of carrying them out in the form in which they were made in August, 1945.
